utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like to ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is case number IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me well? Thank you. As usual, we will do without the appearances, so we can start. [For the Prosecution: Mr. Niemann, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi For the Defence: Mr. Fila, Mr. Petrovic]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we start, Mr. Fila, may I ask you to do me a favour, a favour to all of us? To be careful and ask the witnesses to try to refrain from mentioning names of protected witnesses. Yesterday, you kindly drew my attention, our attention, to the fact that one witness had mentioned the name of a protected witness, so we had to redact the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, let's see where the problem lies. I did not tell those individuals what Witness Q's name is, so if I say not to mention the witness's name, then I have uncovered the witness's identity. Do you see where the problem lies? And if you have a better solution, I will very readily adhere to it, but if I tell him, "Don't tell us the name because it is Witness Q," then that's a difficulty. It is easier for him to say the name and then we can wipe it out, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. But in that case, we can redact the name on the transcript. However, since we are working in this small courtroom and since there is no means of delaying the broadcast of the tape which is being taken, therefore, the public in the public gallery or downstairs, they will hear the name. So therefore, we must go out of our way to make sure that protected witnesses' names are not mentioned. I wonder whether Mr. Niemann has a better idea or any suggestion, a practical suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It might assist, Your Honour, if a mistake happens, rather than mentioning it in open court, to go into private session and then describe what's happened, because often, if something happens like that, it's not so much a problem -- well, it is a problem with it being mentioned -- but that can be exacerbated by discussing it in open court. So if we could immediately go into private session, at some stage go into private session, resolve the matter as best we can, and then come out of private session, I think that would be a better approach to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Good. Thank you. That is a good suggestion. All right. So we may start with the first witness. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Our first witness is Paja Nedic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nedic, could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, did you, on the 16th of September, 1997, make a statement to the investigator on the Defence team, and is that the statement that we're going to show you now? May we have the statement shown here in the courtroom as well, please, and sent to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it your signature on the statement?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there are no objections, then I tender the statement as D108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. There is no objection from the Prosecution, so it's D108.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. It is D109 and D109A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, did you graduate from the machine engineering faculty?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where and when?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I graduated in Belgrade in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in the course of your working career, where you were employed?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: The most part of my career I spent in Bor (phoen), and this was from when I started up to the rank of director of production line in the Bor factory.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Borovo, I'm sorry, the Borovo factory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the Borovo plant represented?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: For the Vukovar region, the Borovo concern was a basic enterprise which employed 75 percent of the working population, which was the social product as well. In the best years of that time, the profits were highest in the Borovo plant, and Borovo was well-known in Europe and the world for producing footwear and for rubber and technical goods and pneumatics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Until what time did you perform your job in the Borovo plant?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: The last day was the 29th of April, 1991. I worked there until that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why was that your last day at Borovo?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: The day before the events that occurred on the 2nd of May in Borovo Selo, and after that, I had a series of informations given to me that I would not be able to go to Borovo and that I must not appear there because at that time unidentified individuals, as they said, could take me away from Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the government of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When were you elected to that function?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I was elected on the 25th of September, 1991, in Beli Manastir, at the assembly that was held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Slavko Dokmanovic a member of that government?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. At that assembly, the government was elected at the proposal of the mandater, and in addition to myself, Slavko Dokmanovic's name was put forward, and with lesser or greater problems, he was elected Minister of Agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were the problems that took place? Who made some problems as to the election of Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, Slavko Dokmanovic's election was attendant with problems. First of all, there were individual members, delegates of the assembly, who, because of Dokmanovic's previous work in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, did not agree with the way in which he worked. They considered that he was one of the people to blame for the position of the Serbian people on that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was he criticised for in concrete terms; do you know?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, he was criticised because he made compromises, first of all with the HDZ, which was one of the parties in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, and also for his cooperation with the organs of the Croatian State.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you known Slavko Dokmanovic personally?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I got to know Slavko Dokmanovic in primary school. We're of the same age, we went to the same primary school, and we went to the same secondary school in part at the same time, and so we attended various village festivities, marriages, sports events. And later on in life, we met frequently. We met frequently at various events and for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us something now about the functioning of the so-called government of the Serbian district of Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, the government of the Serbian district after the elections, in fact, found itself in a situation where it had none of the insignias of function, of parent authority. That is to say, it had no way of using force or the resources it needed, the instruments it needed, in order to function. So it had to make do with what it had at its disposal. There was no electricity at the time, water, no telephone communications. We did not have anywhere to stay, and, in fact, we had to look for chairs to sit on. Some of us found some empty rooms in Erdut which were in a very poor condition and, as I say, we had to bring in chairs quite literally, chairs and tables, and we remained there provisionally, trying to organise what we could under the conditions that prevailed in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that the government partially wanted to establish effective rule in the northern parts of the Serbian district around the Erdut region and that it had no contacts or competences south of the City of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because between Vukovar and Osijek, the territory was in the Serbian villages, we were able to pass through it, and we were not able to go to the eastern part and southern part, south of Vukovar. It was 150 kilometres of road passing through Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which means that there were no territorial links between the northern sections of the Serbian district around Erdut and the part south of the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: That's right. We could not pass through that route on the 25th of November, that is, 1991, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How frequently, as a member of the government, did you meet Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, we had occasion to meet after the 25th of September occasionally in Erdut at joint -- in the rooms which we both used, the halls, and we tried to renovate them to find the chairs and tables and inventory that we needed to function, we tried to introduce a telephone and to have the basics, the bare essentials for us to be able to function. That is where we met, usually in the morning hours. We would comment on the events of the day and we would try to do something to take action, but this was always very difficult because of the prevailing conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps notice what Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing most often in those days?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do, because Slavko was most often wearing a sort of greenish uniform, the hunting type, and part of this clothing was intended for hunters. It was the kind of clothing that hunters wore when they went hunting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If we were to show you that uniform now, could you recognise it, do you think?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I think I could, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you show the witness Exhibit D48, please?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is the clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at it. Take it out and tell us whether that is the clothing worn by him.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the uniform. Whether it was this one -- it was like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it a hunting uniform, the vest, or is it a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: No, this is a hunting uniform. You see, this is intended for the shells, the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you turn this around for the camera to see and for the Chamber to see?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: The cartridges go in there, for example, and this is for a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 19th of November, were you present at the government meeting held in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Slavko Dokmanovic present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We lost that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Why I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please? Could you repeat the answer to the question whether Mr. Dokmanovic was present?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was present at the meeting, and there was a characteristic event which helps me remember that I saw him there and that we talked before the meeting and at the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was that event; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, one of our colleagues --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We lost that.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: -- who was -- who lost his grandparents --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Once again, please, could you --

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I remember the event because one of our colleagues had lost his grandparents, that is to say, the parents of his wife, his in-laws, they were elderly people, and we talked to him about that event. He was in a very difficult situation having lost two people he liked, so I remember that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I should like to show the witness D53, Exhibit D53.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And would you please tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I do not have Exhibit D63 with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, what is that document?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: It is the minutes from the meeting of the government meeting, number 17, of the Serbian district.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that the minutes of the meeting that we're talking about, that is the one held on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you look at page 2 of the minutes, point 5, and would you read it out and explain what it is all about?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: "That the Serbian district be placed above the units of the JNA on its territory." I think that this formulation in point 5 is not adequate and has not been well-expressed and introduced into the text --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you have just said from the beginning, please? Your comment of point 5.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: My comment of point 5 is that this is an inadequate formulation of what is meant, and from this we can see that we are asking to be above the -- superior to the units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That means did you ask for something that you did not have at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't think that we asked to supersede the JNA units at that time either. What we wanted was that after the liberation of certain localities to establish civilian rule, civilian power and authority, and I don't think that the text reflects our ideas. I think that Mr. Jovan Pejakovic, who wrote the minutes, did not express this adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in the places that were liberated there was no civilian rule and that it was under the control of the government of the Serbian district?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not under the control of the Serbian government district, it was a war zone, a war locality, and it was, in fact, the JNA who held power over that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And when were the first organs of civilian power and authority established on the liberated territories?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Only after the liberation of Vukovar, when it was possible for the council of Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Repeat that, please. We lost you.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Only when -- only after the liberation of Vukovar when the executive board was established, executive council was established for Vukovar. Only at that point was this established in other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So until the liberation of the town and the election of the executive council, what way was the town of Vukovar administered and the Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, the town of Vukovar was at the time under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army in practical terms, and the government did not have any power and authority over the town and the administration of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the executive council of the Municipality of Vukovar was formed and when it began to function in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, it was proposed and elected at a government meeting, I think it was on the 28th of November, 1991. But when it began to function in practical terms, perhaps 15 days later, perhaps 30 days later, I'm not quite sure. But the ten individuals who were proposed for the executive council had a lot of problems to contend with, and they were not able to establish civilian rule. This took some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we now go back to the minutes that you have in front of you? And on page 2, the last paragraph notes that the members of the government will, on the following day, have a meeting. Could you read out what it says and explain to us what it says?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: "Goran Hadzic, the Prime Minister, informs the members of the government that due to the situation in Vukovar, it is necessary for the government members to be on Wednesday, the 20th of November, 1991 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We lost the name of where.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: "-- and for Friday, on the 22nd of November, 1991, a meeting, government meeting, was convened in Beli Manastir at 9.00."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain the difference between convening the meeting for Friday and the government members gathering on the 20th in Vukovar? Was there any difference there between the two meetings?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course there was, because at the government meeting to which the material before me relates, we were informed that part of Vukovar had been liberated, and the proposal was that those members of the government who can and who have the necessary transport to go to Vukovar should go there, should appear there, because the government had no way of acting in Vukovar. So this was the first appearance of the government in Vukovar, and no meeting was scheduled there. Perhaps if the people met there, then they could have a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that it was the government's intention to demonstrate its existence by being in Vukovar on the 20th and not to hold a meeting, a regular meeting?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, to have a show of presence for the government because the greatest portion of the government members were not in Vukovar on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it follows on --

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It follows on from there that the regular government meeting was convened for Friday, the Friday mentioned in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was scheduled for the 22nd of November and was held on November the 22nd in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So that is the next government meeting in relation to the 17th that we mentioned. So on Friday, it was the 18th government session; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the meeting or the session that was held in Vukovar on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: No, I did not attend that meeting because at that time it was not an obligatory thing. It was a simple visit to Vukovar which was supposed to enable people to come to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last sentence? Please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: No, it was not an obligation. Most members did not have any transport, so they did not show up there. We had no meeting that was scheduled there. We simply wanted to meet there at a certain point in time, if possible, and I didn't believe that it was necessary for me to go 150 kilometres and to be there because nothing special was supposed to be decided or nothing special was supposed to take place, so I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it means that there was no quorum on that meeting, no agenda, and no minutes were taken during that meeting, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since you know Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic from your early days, could you tell us your opinion about this man?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: He's a friend of mine from a neighbouring village which is only 2 kilometres away from my village. We have known each other very well. And in addition to the time that we spent together in our youth, we also worked as colleagues while he was working in the Vukovar municipality as an expert for agriculture between 1970 and 1980 -- 1980 and 1990. And during that time, he never expressed any kind of radical opinions, he never picked a fight, he never quarrelled with people. He was always acting in an opposite way. He was the one who was trying to make peace with people. He was involved in the public life of the village, and I think he had a considerable influence in resolving differences between villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the family of Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, I know them now. I've known Dan'lka for some time, that's his wife. I think she's about the same age as we are. And, yes, I know her. I didn't spend as much time with her as I spent with Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You have probably heard Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic has been charged with participating in the killing of 200 people. What do you think of that?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: It's impossible, it's simply impossible. This is the kind of man who wouldn't be able to do a much less serious thing, he wouldn't be able to assist in such a thing, be present at such an event. It's a simple mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nedic. The Defence has no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, the minutes of the meeting that you discussed, D53, have you seen those minutes before, I mean, in the witness box today?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why was that? Why wouldn't you have seen them before this?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody offered me to see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps there may be some confusion. I'm talking about, did you see them at around about the time that they were produced back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I tried to find the minutes that I took home. This is not the one that I took home. I haven't seen these minutes. This is not the one I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said that -- expressed doubts about whether the government could have exercised control over the JNA. There's no question, is there, that the government had authority over the Territorial Defence as opposed to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is your question, please? I apologise. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is clear. Can you put it again? But it is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that you expressed doubts about the government's authority to exercise control over the JNA, but there is no question about your ability to exercise authority over the Territorial Defence, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We lost the beginning.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: And there was no possibility to control the Territorial Defence because the assembly had adopted a decision whereby they would be integrated within the armed forces of Yugoslavia as of the beginning of August -- that is October, I'm sorry, from October onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What then is intended or meant by item 2 on these minutes that refer to the Territorial Defence commander?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, practically it says here that the link that existed between the Territorial Defence and the JNA, the liaison officer should report to the government, if this is the item 2. This is the first time, actually, that I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, you know Miroljub Vujovic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I know who that person is, but I cannot say that I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You know him to be a person who was in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, I learned that only after the liberation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I learned that only at the meeting of the government on the 28th and 29th of November when we were deciding as to the membership of the executive council of the Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Miroljub Vujovic was appointed to the executive council of Vukovar by the government, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I mean, I don't have any kind of document that would -- to confirm, but I believe that he was on that list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, at the meeting on the 19th of November, 1991, was there any discussion about what would be the subject of the discussion at the meeting in Vukovar the next day, the 20th?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I have already said that no meeting was supposed to be held in Vukovar but that one part of the government was supposed to go to Vukovar just to see what the situation was, to introduce themselves to the people, to show them that there was government in place. There was no agenda whatsoever and no meeting, no session was held. The session was held on the 22nd of November in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Members of the government had the freedom to choose, did they, whether they would want to go to Vukovar or whether they didn't?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They each could decide for him or herself whether to go. It also depended on the transport available, and I told you, between the western part of the area and Vukovar, you had to cover about 130, 150 kilometres, and at that time, it was by no means easy. It was a difficult distance to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, this freedom of choosing whether or not you should attend, are you sure it had nothing to do with the contents of the discussion which you were to have at Vukovar on that day?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I repeat, it was not obligatory for us to go to Vukovar because no meeting of the government was convened and no agenda had been drafted, and I know very well that the President told us that those who could go should come to Vukovar just to see what was happening and to introduce themselves to the people who would by all means gather there. We had no idea of what was happening in Vukovar at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the period leading up to the 20th of November when you were a member of the government, did you wear a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, I can claim with certainty that I never wore a complete uniform, maybe only a jacket, that is, the upper part of the uniform, and for practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what were the practical reasons that you wore the military jacket?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, the practical reasons were, for example, because I lived in that area between Erdut -- in the area between Erdut and my village, there were at least five or six checkpoints, and every civilian of my age at that time was suspicious, to say the least. Therefore, I had to pass these checkpoints every day, and sometimes even two times a day, and each explanation to whoever was at the checkpoint as to why I was wearing civilian clothes, let alone a tie, which I'm wearing now, this would -- this would most certainly anger the people who were there at the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, this would have also applied, would it not, to other people who were travelling, for example, from Trpinja to Erdut, such as Mr. Dokmanovic's situation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the beginning.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: ... because of the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That was the latter part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I need to repeat the question because we didn't receive it all here in The Hague, so I will repeat the question again, if I may? My question is the necessity to wear at least some part of a military uniform would have also applied to other people, such as Mr. Dokmanovic, who at the time was travelling between Trpinja and Erdut.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: If you haven't heard me, I said yes. I said that he had the same kind of problems I had, and vice versa, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said -- wasn't your evidence that you said there were no telephones at all in Erdut at the time?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: At that time there was, I think, one telephone line, which was busy from time to time, and there was one telephone, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Nedic, I have one or two questions for you. You said, in answering a question put to you by Defence counsel, that there was no quorum at the meeting in Vukovar on the 20th of November. How do you know that there was no quorum? You were not there. Did somebody tell you afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Two days later, on the 22nd of November, in Beli Manastir, the people who had been to Vukovar, who had visited Vukovar, we knew who these people were, and as I told you, I believe that most members of the government could not go and were not there in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore I understand from what you say that you were told on the 22nd of November, at the subsequent meeting of the government, that no quorum existed in Vukovar on the 20th. That means that those people who had participated in the meeting on the 20th reported to you and other members who had been absent on the 20th of November about what had been discussed on the 20th. What were you told about the matters discussed on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, seven years later, I think it's very difficult for anyone to remember exactly what happened. Those who were in Vukovar told us about the situation in the town. This is something I could tell you about. But as for the meeting, whether any kind of meeting was held, I cannot -- I cannot tell you. It was a long time ago. But these people went to Vukovar just to see the condition of the town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: However, they did tell you about a small detail of the meeting, namely, that no quorum existed, there was no quorum in the meeting. They dwelt on a small detail and didn't report to you on the major problem of what had been discussed and possibly agreed upon on the 20th. Don't you find this a bit odd, that there was a difference between this detail and the major matters? Sorry. I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, nobody mentioned any kind of quorum, and this is the conclusion I made on the basis of who went there, and my conclusion was that there was no quorum. On the other hand, I can tell you that what we discussed on the 22nd of November in Beli Manastir was just impressions that people had made during their visit to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question: What was the practice of your government as far as the taking of minutes was concerned? Were minutes taken by somebody present at the meeting? I imagine that this was so. But were they formally read out and adopted at the meeting or at the subsequent meeting?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Well, usually the person who was in charge of taking minutes, it was Jovan Pejakovic, in most cases it was him, and afterwards that document would be taken to Dalj where they had a typewriter and then he would draft -- he would make a draft of the minutes; and on the following meeting, he would distribute it, if possible, to all present and all members. We were supposed to have a look at it and to confirm whether this corresponded to the contents of the previous meeting, previous session, and we would, after that, adopt the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Does this imply that on the 22nd of November, the minutes of the meeting on the 20th of November, were adopted, were read by all members of government and adopted by them?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Of the 20th of November? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, you're right. I apologise. I made a mistake. I meant to say the minutes of the meeting of the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Were they circulated on the 22nd of November to all members of government and adopted by them in that meeting of the 22nd of November?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: No. No, they were not distributed on the 22nd of November, maybe later, maybe sometime after that, but they were not circulated on that day because a meeting of the government in Beli Manastir preceded the session, and there was a lot of materials, a lot of documents that had to be prepared, and I'm quite sure that no agenda was proposed at that time for adoption during that session of the government, the one that was held in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. This is in spite of the fact that the minutes were actually taken -- I mean typewritten on the 20th of November, 1991, at Dalj, as we can see from this document produced by Defence counsel, D53. You have got it in front of you, and you may see there that it carries the date of the 20th of November. That means that they were drafted on the 20th at Dalj. So my assumption was -- I thought that they had been therefore discussed on the 22nd. But probably it was not so, according to you. They were not discussed and adopted on the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: PAJA NEDIC
utterances.text: I believe, and I'm almost sure, that no, that they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions? No? All right. There is no objection to Mr. Nedic being released? Mr. Nedic, thank you for testifying. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogdan Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, good morning. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, on the 26th of November, 1998, did you make a statement? You will be shown the statement. Is it your statement, the statement that you made and signed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 26th I made this statement, and I remain completely in accord with the statement as I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there are no objections, then I would like to tender it into evidence. The next number, is it 110? I suppose it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is document D110 and D110A for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, can you tell us, please, something about your education, what schools you completed, where and when?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of economics in Zagreb in 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your working career, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: From 1972 until the end of 1989, I worked in Vupik, Vukovar, and the last ten years there, I was the financial director of Vupik, and from the beginning of 1990, I formed a private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the government of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What function did you perform?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: From the 25th of September, I held the function of Finance Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Slavko Dokmanovic a member of that government as well?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic was a member of the government, yes, and he was in charge of Agriculture, he was Minister of Agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the daily functioning of that government, whether the government had everything that is understood as being part of a regular government? Did it have its secretariats, its administrative organs, were the members given salaries and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, taking into account the conditions under which the government functioned, in practical terms, for the most part, it was not able to perform its functions in a regular way. There were not enough financial resources, and also the general situation in the area was such that it was not able to function, so that it was declarative in nature for the public and for the people, whereas the true functions performed by government, it was not able to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation in the area? You mentioned the situation.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time that the government was formed, war operations were still underway. That is on the one hand. Secondly, the government had a rather bad image vis-à-vis the population because the greatest part of the people who were members of the government in the course of May and June had left the area for different reasons. They had left with their families. And I think that it is this factor which is essential as well when looking at the government's image. And also it was not able to have control over the section such as Baranja, Dalj, Erdut, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What locality did the government control, if we can say that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, conditionally speaking, it controlled Baranja and the area around Erdut, Dalj, Borovo Selo, and all the Western Srem region, which means from Vukovar towards the border, and Ilok, towards Ilok and Sid, it had no control, no competences over that locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that Slavko Dokmanovic was also a member of the government. Can you tell us how long you have known Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've known Slavko Dokmanovic from the mid 1970s, because we worked in the same enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that you worked in the same enterprise. What kind of worker was Slavko Dokmanovic? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I had a leading function in the firm, we very often spoke about the cadres, the personnel that we had at our disposal. We had 120 university graduates. And Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic was a highly esteemed man as a professional for the area in which he was a professional, and also he was highly respected as a man, as a personality, because it was a mixed enterprise, which means that there were Croats and Serbs employed there, but we didn't pay attention to who was what nationality. But at certain moments here and there, if some conflict situations would break out, he was always very reasonable in trying to quell passions, not only political conflicts but others as well. So he was a man who was very reasonable, conciliatory, and always ready to find a way out and to help people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the details concerning the election of Dokmanovic for Minister in the government?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said a moment ago, I spoke about the image of the government, and as the assembly was made up of individuals mostly from the villages and the government members had fled from the area, then for certain individuals, there was problems of the elections, partially for myself as well. However, for Slavko Dokmanovic, Slavko Dokmanovic had a fairly poor image starting out from the fact that his behaviour, his conduct in 1991 was seen to be a traitor to Serbian interests, that he had betrayed Serbian interests, and he was criticised as the President of the Municipal Assembly for allowing the police station to move from Vukovar to Vinkovci and the internal affairs unit, and he was also criticised for leaving the National Council, he was criticised publicly, the council that was set up in Srb, and so he was anathema on the part of many Serbs. So that there were considerable problems regarding his election as a member of the government. However, at the intervention of Mr. Hadzic who, on two occasions, had to take the rostrum and speak about his professional qualities because it was to be a government with members who did not deal in politics alone but were professionals in their own right and were respected as professionals in their particular spheres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you yourself had some problems in the elections for a government member. Could you tell us what that was all about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 26th of August, I left Vukovar with my family and I lived in Novi Sad, and it was only at Goran Hadzic's invitation prior to the formation of the government that I came from there and, of course, all the people who had remained in the area. I was treated as not having protected Serbian interests sufficiently. That was the attitude towards us and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you, on the 26th of August, 1991, leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So not August but June.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It was in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. What date did you leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was common knowledge, and with the victory of the HDZ and HDZ coming into power, there were verbal pressures exerted, first of all, and then the media of the Republic of Croatia began to exert pressure either through the official government representatives on the position and status of the Serbs and the difficult situation that they would encounter in times to come. On the other hand, there was a lot of pressure exerted, telephone conversations, threats --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, speech is very intermittent at the moment.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: There was obstruction by the police. And after May the 2nd --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's very difficult to follow now. Intermittent speech. We can't follow.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The National Guard members came. There was daily shooting during the day as well as during the night.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we can't hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian houses were set fire to as well as businesses. (Pause in proceedings)

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, I hope you can hear me now.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can hear you perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us go back to when you left Vukovar. When was that and why?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I left Vukovar on the 28th of June together with my family. The reason I left Vukovar -- there were several reasons. In the course of 1990, there were verbal pressures brought to bear against the Serbian population, either on the part of the official authorities or via the media, public information media. I considered that it was not -- the situation was not yet critical if it was only verbal pressure. However, at the beginning of 1991, there was an escalation of pressure on the Serb population. It began with people being sacked from work, replaced from leading functions, there was gunfire in the town, both during the day and during the night. And after the 2nd of May, Serbian facilities were shelled, blown up. Can you hear me? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Serbian businesses and houses, there were killings, as happened in Sotin, Brsadin, in Vukovar, and at the same time, the civilians took up arms, they were members of the HDZ, and they went out into the streets of Vukovar, and there was a concentration of the members of the National Guard, the Zengas, and in addition to the other historical emotional reasons that I don't want to go into at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many people left Vukovar at the time that you're talking about, the Serbs, I have in mind?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to make an assessment because this migration began in March 1991 and went on to the middle or end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you do not have the precise data, can we say that the majority of the population left Vukovar or remained in Vukovar? I'm speaking about the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we must take a look at the population structure, and we must be conscious of the fact that the pressure was exerted on the prominent Serbs, for the most part, whether they had private businesses, the owners of private businesses, or those working in different firms; and over 80 percent of those people, those prominent Serbs, had left Vukovar. It is difficult to expect pensioners, elderly pensioners to leave, and they probably did not feel that pressure. They might have felt it emotionally but not physically. It was the prominent Serb citizens who felt the pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, were you at the government meeting that was held in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit D53, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at this document, please, sir, and tell us what it is about? What is the document before you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It is the minutes from the meeting held -- it is the 17th session held on the 19th of November, 1991, in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about that document? Can we see from the document that it was a government meeting in question? Does it show that at the government meeting there was a set agenda? Can we see from the document that the agenda was put forward and then adopted by the government members? Does it show who was present at the meeting? Could you tell us about those technical elements of the minutes, please?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that you said can be seen in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So there was a set agenda which was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how was the agenda determined?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The agenda was usually determined by an invitation to attend the meeting or, at the meeting itself, if the invitations were not -- could not be handed out to the majority of government members, then it was read out at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at page 2 of the minutes and the conclusions that were adopted? We are particularly interested in item 5 of the adopted conclusions. Would you read it out and tell us what you can --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Once again, please. We lost that.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I do not recall that this conclusion was brought in. But if this is the official minutes and if the minutes state this, then it must have been, but I do not think that this conclusion could have been implemented under the prevailing conditions because the situation was quite different at the given time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether there were any contacts between the government of the district and the army, command of the army units, whether they had an exchange of information between the two structures and whether there was a relationship of subordination between the government and the JNA, the JNA and the government? How did all this function?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I was informed and at the meetings that I attended, there were no official contacts of this kind. Now, whether some individual members of the government did, in fact, contact JNA units, I can't say. I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the units of the JNA who were in the locality of the Serbian district, did they take orders from the government of the Serbian district?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA units have any responsibility about informing of their plans or the actions undertaken?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not have this responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the areas which were liberated after the war operations had come to an end, was military rule established or was there civilian power and authority?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for a certain time, there was military rule, military administration, but we succeeded later on in setting up an executive council in the Vukovar region; for example, this was somewhere at the end of November or the beginning of December. However, there were some major problems in this respect. It was difficult -- things were difficult for civilian administration to be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was civilian administration established in the Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It was somewhere at the end of December, I believe, but only in set areas, not everywhere, and set --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In set areas? Territorially speaking or for the departments?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the departments and activities of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Production organisation, the organisation of supplies for the civilian population because, you know, it was winter. There was no heating, there was not enough food. And for the most part, in respect to the material resources that we had, we were not able to satisfy needs, fully to satisfy needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at item 3 of the minutes now, please, in the document that you have before you, and tell us what item 3 is about? What did you agree upon in item 3?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Item 3, in item 3, we agreed on the following day, that is to say, on the 20th of November, to hold a meeting of those members of the government who wanted and were able to come to Vukovar, and the basic reason for bringing in this decision, making that conclusion, was to improve the government's image vis-à-vis the public because the government image was very bad, particularly with regard to the Vukovar population, in relation to the Vukovar population. And we also wanted to discuss possibilities for organising production and supplies for the civilian population and to see how matters stood, what the situation was actually like in Vukovar. However, the meeting was not binding, was not obligatory, and it was not an official government meeting because many members did not come. They were not able to go to Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat? Could you repeat the last sentence, please? Could you repeat the last sentence? You said --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Not all the members of the government attended. They could either not come because they were prevented from coming or they considered that it was not necessary for them to come because it was only at the following meeting that we were to discuss the situation in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For a meeting of the members of the government to be called an official meeting, what conditions must be fulfilled for it to be a government session?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is -- invitations must be sent out officially, containing an agenda, because every government member was duty-bound to -- they had certain tasks with regard to the agenda; that is to say, either to determine the agenda at the session itself and keep the minutes and to get the minutes for the next session (sic) and to adopt the minutes or not adopt the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That is to adopt the agenda of the previous session?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is necessary for government decisions to be valid? Do you need to --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You must have the members of the government present and that the proposed conclusions be adopted by the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you, on the 20th of November, attend the meeting of the government members in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many government members attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you an exact figure because it was seven years ago, which is a long time. I can remember some of the names, such as Goran Hadzic, Vitomir Devetak, Susa Vojin, (redacted), Bogdan Vorkapic, I was there myself, and I think Mr. Koncarevic was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Dokmanovic at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dokmanovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us begin with the 20th. When did you arrive in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived somewhere before 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you arrive? Where did you come to?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The administrative building of the VELEPROMET in Vukovar, which is at the entrance to Vukovar from the Negoslavci route.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic in VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that Mr. Dokmanovic attended the meeting that was held in the VELEPROMET building. Could you tell us precisely where the meeting was held? VELEPROMET is a large compound.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the room in the hall within the VELEPROMET enterprise of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which building; do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the entrance. On the left-hand side, you had the porter's lodge and, on the right-hand side, the building that the meeting was held in. The first door was the entrance door to the hall where the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Slavko Dokmanovic present throughout the meeting that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, nobody left the room during the meeting, and Slavko Dokmanovic was present. I know that he even took the floor in connection with the autumn sowing season and as regards to the produces of Vukovar and sowing, harvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Prime Minister, Goran Hadzic, left the meeting at any time, the government meeting, the meeting that was held?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly he left the hall because he usually left the hall to make statements for the press during previous meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did the meeting last?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think it lasted about one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the meeting end; could you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It ended sometime after 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I had come from the direction of Sid, and I went -- I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On that day, when was the last time that you saw Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: After the meeting was completed, I saw him once again, we greeted each other, we said good-bye to each other and members of the government, and we also agreed as to when and where to hold the next meeting, that is the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how Slavko Dokmanovic was dressed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the members of the government at that time were not wearing civilian clothes because they lived in that area and -- you know that it was a very difficult time for them, there was no electricity, no water, et cetera, so Mr. Dokmanovic was also wearing some kind of green uniform. Whether this was a hunting uniform or something else, I don't know, but he was not wearing civilian clothes. He wore some kind of greenish multi-coloured uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since you've known Mr. Dokmanovic for quite a while, could you tell us something about him?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I already stated in my responses that he was very well-respected in the company as he was a good expert for agriculture and that he was also respected amongst the village population because I used to go to his village for football matches and all kinds of village festivities, meetings, meetings of the plant in Trpinja, for example. He was a very rational, realistic man, of a conciliatory nature, both as a worker in his company and as a politician who carried out various functions in that period. You must bear in mind the fact that Slavko Dokmanovic was accepted as President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, he was elected President, although half of the government was Croatian, there were 50 percent Croats and 50 percent Serbs, so he was accepted by both of them, and if he had not been accepted by both of them, he couldn't have been elected President of the Municipal Assembly, which was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back for a while, and I would like Defence Exhibit 48 to be shown to the witness, and I would kindly ask the witness to tell us what this thing is, and I would like the witness to tell us whether these were the clothes that Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing on the 20th of November and also on prior occasions that you met him and later on as well.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like this uniform. I cannot be 100 percent sure about the pattern and colours, but this is the kind of uniform he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that before the International Criminal Tribunal, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic has been charged with participation in the killing of 200 people at Ovcara. Could you give us your comment about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that Slavko did that, and there are two reasons for my belief: First of all, because of his public image, he was the kind of person that could not show up at Ovcara because I believe that most of the Serbs who happened to be there would have killed him as well. And the second reason is his emotional and mental set-up and his character that he demonstrated in previous occasions and in connection with events that had taken place before that in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now take a 20-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All rise. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, are you able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you appointed the Minister of Finance for the government of the Serbian District of Eastern Slovenia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who was it that actually appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly of the government of the Serbian District of Baranja, Eastern Slovenia, Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you a member of that government prior to September?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the government operate and exist prior to September?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Since I lived in Novi Sad at the time, until the invitation by Mr. Hadzic to join the government, I was not aware of that. I was not aware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you joined the government, are you able to tell us how often the government met in order to have its meetings?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually every 10 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And at these meetings were all the Ministers present or were there occasions when there were meetings of lesser than the full number of Ministers?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Most often not all Ministers were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you had meetings, did you have people attend, who were not government ministers, to advise you on current matters, such as the general military situation in the district?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: People who were in charge of military issues were not present, people who coordinated with the JNA. However, Assistant Ministers were present and Presidents of local communes were present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You had a Minister for military matters, didn't you, someone who was responsible for military matters, a Minister for Defence?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, we had a person like that within the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the Minister for Defence, was he the person that would brief the government on the current military situation? And I am talking generally in the autumn and late part of 1991.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he would inform us about the situation, but most often we knew about the situation through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you speak of attending this meeting at Erdut on the 19th of November 1991. What time of day did the meeting take place? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was held in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you remember where it was held, actually, in Erdut, what part of Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held in a resort in Erdut which belonged to a company, IPK, from Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you've had a look at the minutes of that meeting, Exhibit D53. Would you look at that exhibit again for me, please. Can I take you to the final -- it's the last page on my version, but it's at the end of item 2. There is a series of five paragraphs following item 2, starting, "The following conclusions were unanimously adopted". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, looking at paragraph numbered 1, what was the nature of the Proclamation that was going to be given to the citizens of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and again it all happened seven years ago, we had to have a Proclamation to the effect that the citizens should remain calm, that they should not destroy property, because each war implies looting and similar incidents, so in that sense we wanted to react. The winter was approaching and we had to survive the oncoming -- the upcoming winter, and I think that the Proclamation pointed in that sense, in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when was it intended that this Proclamation would be made? What day or date?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't remember that at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think it may have been intended to be proclaimed on the 20th of November, the next day when you went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You seem rather certain about that. Why?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because simply the Proclamation was supposed to be disseminated through the media, and at that time in Vukovar such things did not function. There were no media in Vukovar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was no members of the media attended Vukovar on that day, the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: There were representatives of the media, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, then, this was something that would have needed to have been done reasonably --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but this is one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Proclamation is something that the government would have been anxious to have proclaimed rather urgently, wouldn't you, as a government? You wouldn't have wanted to sit around on something like this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Caslavocic, Mr. Ilija Petrovic, as far as I remember, were not present at the meeting, and at the same time were not able to draft it. So even if we wanted to make a public Proclamation, we didn't have it. They were supposed to draft it and at the same time the Proclamation was supposed to pass through the government for adoption, and only after that it could be made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can we move onto the next item, if we can, number 2. Now, there's a reference there to the Blue Helmets, which are UN forces. Do you see that? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are having some difficulties at the moment. We've lost the sound of your voice, unfortunately. So if you would just bear with us for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You may have sound back again. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think that the witness can hear us, but we cannot hear anything. (Pause in proceedings)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Vojnovic? Can you hear me now Mr. Vojnovic? Can you hear me now Mr. Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry about that. Mr. Vojnovic, the second paragraph relates to the government's views regarding a proposal of sending in the Blue Helmets. Can you tell me, what were the views of the government on that, and perhaps you might just give us a bit of background to it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Again, as far as I remember, the government did accept the arrival of Blue Helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was a proposal that UN forces would be sent into the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Such was the proposal, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vojnovic, it's true, is it not, that there was a distinction to be made between the JNA -- at that particular time between the JNA operating in the Republic Serbia as opposed to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll just go to paragraph 3, if we might. That speaks there of a range of joint meetings with the Republic -- representatives of the Republic of Serbia and the JNA. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 5 you speak of the JNA units being subordinate to the government of the Serbian District, that is your government? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, isn't it the position that you wanted to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, when the Prosecutor is quoting paragraph 5, item 5, he said that they were above the JNA units, that they will be. I would kindly ask to make the distinction between the tenses. They are, as opposed to they will be. Please kindly bear this in mind when you ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't understand the objection, Your Honour. I understand his words. I don't understand his meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We were told by the Defence Counsel and the interpreters that actually this document in item 5 -- is it item 2.5 is mistranslated. It should read as follows, "That JNA units shall be subordinate to the Serbian District on its territory." Not "are", "shall be".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the fact that I suggested anything else, other than future tense. Thank you. I may have misspoke, Your Honour. If that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In any event it doesn't matter. The point I am making, isn't it true that the JNA units were to be subordinated to the government of the Serbian district, and in order to achieve that, you wanted to have discussions with the Republic of Serbia and the JNA, and so that the two items were linked?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Even if we wanted to have that kind of meeting, if the government -- in view of the functions that it had, I don't think that such a meeting ever took place. This was a simple wish, for the government to be above the JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, you had a Minister of Defence who presumably would have some sort of a military formation under his control, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not, because the formations that were at our disposals were simply non-existent. We did have village guards organised in Serbian villages, who had been organised on their own, and the government had no influence whatsoever over those village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about Mr. Arkan's forces; were they at your disposal at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Vukovar on the 21st of November, 1991, where did you leave from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: From Sid via Orolik and towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you see -- first see Mr. Dokmanovic when you went to Vukovar on that day?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him sometime around 1.00 p.m. After 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who was he with? Did you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: He was with Rade Leskovac, and he was also with the representatives of the Kladovo Municipality, representatives of Jagodina, because before the war Vukovar and Svetozarevo had been twin cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On that day were you dressed in a military uniform or were you in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you give us -- was it a suit or a tie or can you give us a description as best you can of what you were wearing?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, it was not a suit and a tie, of course not. I had a simple shirt, a pullover and a jacket. And because I did not live in the area of that particular district, but in Novi Sad where conditions were much more favourable than there, yes, this was the kind of clothes I was wearing that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And during the time that you were with the government, at all stages did you wear civilian clothes, did you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
