utterances.text: Now, when you attended the government meeting on the 20th of November at VELEPROMET, apart from government members who were there, what military personnel attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the meeting was attended by a Colonel of the JNA who was presiding over the meeting, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think his surname is Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it, no relation to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. We come from different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And apart from Colonel Vojnovic, was there any other military person there, either from the JNA or other military personnel?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, there were no other such members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about Arkan, was he there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said that the government image at that time was poor, particularly in relation to the population of Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Not quite poor, but it was not good either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And that was because people such as -- well, the government and people such as Mr. Dokmanovic hadn't adopted a hard line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so one of the objectives of this meeting that you sought to achieve was to demonstrate, especially to the people of Vukovar, that the government was now about to get tough?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you that this was what you were trying to achieve, and that this is why you took a decision at this meeting to make sure that all the extremists from the Croatian side, as you would have called them, were dealt with summarily?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when I used the expression Croatian extremist. Are you referring to me? I mean, this is not something that was on our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I'm just putting it to you that that's what the discussion was about; the discussion was about getting tough in dealing with people from the Croatian side who you saw as being the perpetrators of this military action?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: But we didn't have any kind of competences or possibilities to act, because this was all within the authority, within the control of the JNA. We could only deal with civilian issues, and even that was not possible for us to carry out in an efficient manner, let alone military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did members of the government, during the time that you were at VELEPROMET, inspect or go and see Croatian persons who were being held as prisoners in any part of the VELEPROMET complex?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that detail. During the meeting nobody left the room. I don't know whether anything happened after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that there were people there who were being detained by either the JNA or the Territorial Defence at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that, and it was not possible for us to move around freely. We simply -- we went directly to the room from the gate, because we had to pass a number of checkpoints before the gate. We were supposed to show documents in order to get into Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once you were in Vukovar, though, was it possible for you to drive around and look at the state of the destruction, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you are saying. I was not able to do that, and I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why weren't you able to do it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, simply I didn't dare to move around. I simply stuck to VELEPROMET and I wanted to go back as soon as possible. Whether a government member was able to do that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that after the meeting on the 20th of November at VELEPROMET you then met momentarily with the members of the government and agreed on the time and venue of your next meeting; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I said that we had said good-bye to each other because the next -- the meeting had already been agreed upon and we agreed that the meeting would be held on the 22nd in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why wasn't there records kept of this meeting of the government?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Because this was not a working meeting of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But, surely, if the ministers of the government get together and have a meeting and there are representatives from the JNA present, that's a significant event, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't even know that we would meet with the representatives of the JNA. When we arrived to the room, this JNA Colonel was already there, and the government was not supposed to move around Vukovar the way they wanted. So, as I told you, there was several controls, several check-ups already at the arrival, and at the gate to VELEPROMET we had -- there was a checkpoint, and only after we had shown them our documents we were then allowed to proceed to the room where the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How could you possibly have hoped to make an impression upon the people of the City of Vukovar as a government, if you met in private, behind closed doors, and you kept no record of what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't even know what the situation in Vukovar was. We saw that the situation would be more or less normal, that we would be able to move freely around the town of Vukovar. We were rather surprised when we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said that you didn't believe that Mr. Dokmanovic would go to the Ovcara farm, because if he did the Serbs there would kill him. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that he didn't dare go there, because he had a very poor image, because of all the events that had taken place beforehand, between 1980 and the take-over by the Croatian government, when he was replaced by the Croatian government as President. So that was the reason that I offered to you, the reason as to why he didn't dare show up at Ovcara, let alone decide about anything that was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, if he wanted to change his conciliatory image, one of the best ways he could have done that, wouldn't it, would be to go to Ovcara on that day?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, because passions were running high at this time, and for him this would have been the worst possible moment to do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minor thing in the last response to -- the last answer to one of the questions of Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A reference is made to the period between 1980 and the take-over. I presume that the witness had the year of 1990?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And one more thing. You said that the next meeting was convened, from the 22nd, Friday, in Erdut. Could you please have a look at the transcript that is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 of the minutes where it says where the next government -- the next meeting of the government was supposed to be convened. I presume that you misspoke when you said Erdut instead of Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't understand. The minutes are from the 19th of November, so on that meeting it was agreed where the next meeting of the government would take place, that is on the 22nd of November 1991 in Erdut at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out item 3.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: "Goran Hadzic, President of the government, is hereby informing members of the government that it is necessary, due to the situation in Vukovar, for the members of government to assemble on Wednesday, 20th of November, in Vukovar. At Friday, 22nd of November, a meeting, a session of the government is being convened in Beli Manastir at 9.00."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, therefore, we are talking about Beli Manastir, not Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't misspeak?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: One more clarification. Throughout this time, throughout the existence of the government of the Serbian District, did you live in Novi Sad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I gather there is no objection to the witness being released? Thank you so much for giving evidence. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I suggest that maybe we start with one more witness. Yes, we have some time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is witness Milos Vojnovic, and I asked your permission to question the witness yesterday, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, good morning. Could you please stand and read out the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, will you tell us your name and your surname, what school qualifications you have, where you graduated and when?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milos Vojnovic. I graduated from the Faculty of Law in Belgrade in 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you live in Vukovar in the period that we are interested in, that is to say 1990 to 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have been living in Vukovar since 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you live there now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I live there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were you by profession in 1990, 1991? What job did you hold?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was a judge in the Municipal Court in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you leave Vukovar in 1991, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I left Vukovar on the 24th of May, 1991 because I was made to do so -- persecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they try to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that day at about 9.30 my colleague was arrested in the court. He is Sretiac Slavoljub. He was a judge as well. And somewhere at around on noon on the same day, the representatives of the Croatian police came to arrest me, but due to certain problems that arose as to identity, identification, this did not happen. And in the afternoon hours of that same day I was cautioned that there would be a fresh attempt to arrest me, and then with the help of some friends and acquaintances I succeeded in fleeing from Vukovar. And somewhere around 6 p.m. on that same day they came to my flat to arrest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you and Judge Slavoljub have immunity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We had immunity, as proclaimed by the Republic of Croatia, if I recall correctly, and a lot of time has gone by, usually for criminal acts related to performing our professional functions. I do not know whether this immunity was limited to that or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the political forces have any authority to take away this immunity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, they had nothing in writing, no written warrants or any other documents, apart from their professional ID's, which they used to identify themselves with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the function of President of the Court exist?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What nationality was he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: He was Petar Mrksic and he was a Serb by nationality, an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened to him? Was he replaced? Was he relieved of his duty?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was replaced. He was replaced sometime -- in those days after our suspension. I don't know the exact date. I think that it was at the end of May, but otherwise he was a very successful court president and performed his functions for more than ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you repeat the name of the president of the court, his nationality, why he was replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: His name is Petar Mrksic. He was a Serb by nationality and he was replaced for three official reasons. If I recall, it was stated that he waged a bad cadres policy, personnel policy, that he did not work sufficiently in solving concrete cases before him, and that there were very poor inter-human relations in the court. Of course, none of this was correct because the Court of Vukovar under his leadership was one of the most successful courts to function in with the Republic of Croatia. So it was his national affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, after leaving Vukovar, did you in the government of SAO, which was set up later on, did you hold a function in that government?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In the second half of August, I don't exactly remember the date, I think it was towards the end of August, I was called by some people to be included into some processes that were ongoing and topical at the time. And after the so-called government, to call it that, was set up, I was given the post of assistant for jurisprudence for the Justice Department, if I recall, and I think I do because I was present. That was on the 25th of September 1991? In Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whose deputy were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was assistant, not deputy, but assistant. The assistant to Mr. Susa Vojin. He was the Justice Minister, Vojin, Susa. Yes, that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What functions did you perform later on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, a short time later, I think on the 9th of October, 1991, the judges were elected for that locality and I was chosen -- elected President of the Provincial Regional Court. It was the sort of top instance institution of justice. And there were no more operations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I say that it is true that there were Regional Courts and Municipal Courts?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They weren't called that, but that was in fact what they were, that you had the Basic court, you had the Higher Court and the Regional Court, the Provincial Court. And it was the judges who were elected on that day, the 9th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did that Justice Department come into effect, if it ever did?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to confront a series of problems right at the very start, both legal problems and technical problems, so that the process of implementation and translation into practice lasted a long time, and apart from the fact that we were formed, it was in 1992 that we began to function seriously as a court. But we were present there before that because it was considered that on territories where there were no war operations that an institution of this kind should exist of an exclusively civilian nation, so that we could see to law and order and for that institution to have the power of jurisprudence and jurisdiction. But it was a slow and unwieldy process.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you perform the functions of justice in the Srpska Krajina region?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remained in my post until April or May of 1996 when, due to the prevailing circumstances, I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When I entered the realm of politics in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were you before that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was President of the Regional Court and afterwards of the Supreme Court, when the courts conjoined.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What function do you hold at the present time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I am president of the Joint Council -- we didn't hear -- of Eastern Slovenia, Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Within the composition of the present Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a component part of the Republic of Croatia and the Joint Council is an institution which was set up by the Erdut meeting as an institution by which the Serbs should articulate some of their rights and interests. Therefore, it is not an organ or parent authority, but a political consultancy, administrative institution, and we maintain continuous contacts with the Croatian institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who elected you to that post and how were you elected?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was elected by the Joint Council. It is a collective body having 50 representatives from all the municipalities of the area west -- inhabited by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, I have been asking you all this for one reason. Do you know that in the course of your career, legal career, somebody has been convicted of a war crime in the area of Srpska Krajina, Beli Manastir, or was somebody charged?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, charged and sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And is he still carrying out that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I have for two years left this legal department and I don't know his fate, but I can't recall -- and I can't recall his name and surname at the moment, but he was sentenced to 20 years imprisonment, and that sentence was confirmed and is legally binding for legal -- criminal acts performed to the detriment of the people of Hungarian and other Croatian nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any other instances of persecution of the Serb nationality for criminal acts against Croats, Hungarians, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at this point in time I think there were, but I cannot recall, because I was in the Supreme Court, and this was done -- these were cases that came before the lower courts. So I can't speak of the individual cases, but I do believe that such cases did exist. Thank you. But our general orientation was, for the most part, classical crimes, and of course of the civilian part of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, do you know an inhabitant of Vukovar called Berghofer, Dragutin Berghofer?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have known him for many years, and I can say that I have known him on three counts; that is to say, I know him from the time that he worked in an enterprise in Vukovar to which I came. I was head of the legal service of that particular firm. I think it was in 1979. And later on I met him again --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We lost that, I'm afraid. We lost what he said.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: He had a lot of --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We heard about the first count, we heard how you first met him, but we didn't hear what you said after that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We know him as somebody who came before the courts as a -- as civil parties and he appeared in these court cases. I was a civilian judge and dealing with property cases in which he appeared as a party in cases -- alimony, cases concerning alimony and family law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to any evidence -- I object to any evidence given by a judge of a litigant before that judge in relation to a witness in these proceedings, if that's what the purpose of this evidence is. I submit, Your Honours, that it's highly inappropriate and improper for a judge to come before this Tribunal and testify about proceedings that have gone on before that judge in a case that he might have dealt with in his capacity as a judge. In my respectful submission, it demeans the Tribunal to receive and accept that evidence, especially if it's a matter that goes to the character of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask the witness in that case about what he learned about Mr. Berghofer outside his duty as a judge? Nothing to do with himself as a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, don't speak about the lawsuits, but how do you know him on the third count you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was not going to speak about the individual lawsuits. I just said that I met him as a party in the court. I did not wish to speak of individual suits, because you are duty bound not to speak about lawsuits, and I will not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that is in answer to the objection raised.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, I met Mr. Berghofer again as somebody who likes football, as a football fan, amateur football fan. I played football for many years and we met on the sports fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What kind of man was he? What was his character? Was he respected?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a psychiatrist, and it is difficult for me to say. But all I can tell you is that amongst us he was considered to be somebody of a freer conduct and behaviour and relationship towards his responsibilities. I don't want to enter into any other qualifications which might step out of the frameworks of a general --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We didn't hear the last part.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: -- communications between citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, carry on. Do you know whether he said the truth? Was he known as somebody who always talked and said the truth or was inclined to make things up or exaggerate matters?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I say, he was freer in his conduct, in his behaviour, and gave the impression of somebody who was not always serious. He was not always a serious person.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you say he was freer in his conduct, in his behaviour, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think he was criminal in his conduct, but he was very free in going about the town, very sort of liberal. He talked to people. Not very serious. For example, one detail: When I came to the enterprise that I worked in, that he had left his job because he didn't wish to accept a more serious technological and work discipline that the new leadership and I amongst it insisted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean he wasn't a good worker?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time when I came to the enterprise, he was considered to be a pretty poor worker, and as we insisted on technological and working discipline, he did not like that, and he left the enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that he told various stories and that he was not always serious. What do you mean by that that? Were they false stories?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were usually humorous stories, jokes, sports topics, talk on sports topics and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And as a family man, can you tell us something about that? Did he take care of his family? Was he a responsible family man?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I am going to disclose any secrets. It is a well-known fact that he divorced his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We don't want anything from court practice, just what you know privately. Only privately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, to what extent is this relevant to our case? His family life, I mean, that's nothing to do with our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So let us summarise. You have given us certain qualifications of the man?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: As I experienced him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you give us a definition of whether it is somebody to be believed? Is he a man to be believed? Was he a well respected man amongst you all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, amongst us he was considered to be somebody who liked to joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A little bit of a charlatan, perhaps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Niemann, do you think you need to put many questions, because we could carry on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't think I need to put any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No questions. All right. Mr. Vojnovic, thank you for testifying. You may now be released. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We may now adjourn and we'll reconvene at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have two witness -- only two witnesses for this afternoon, so you can plan your day quite easily. No tension there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you mean only two through video link?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No video links at all. No more video links. Just two witnesses here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So that both Gradina and Leskovac have dropped out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They haven't turned up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we have Susa Vojin and Zlatic Radoslav?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. And they are waiting to be heard here. And the Colonel that I mentioned, I will be able to question only tomorrow, not before tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What about the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He has brought this material, these documents with him, so I would like to leave that for tomorrow. Those are the documents that he was brought with him that I have to examine. As far as expert witnesses are concerned, we have a translation of the document, you will be receiving it in the course of the day, and he will be heard after Mr. Dokmanovic's statement. So that the plan is as follows: I complete the two witnesses today, if Your Honours agree, tomorrow we are going to start off with the Colonel, because he has brought documents with him that I have asked to see, and they have seen fit to give me those documents. And then afterwards I would like to start with Mr. Dokmanovic and probably the day after the expert witness. And that would complete my case, as I promised you. The only thing is that I have a new task governing the circumstances -- concerning the penalty which I was not able to complete. So I need one extra day or a day and a half in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Because we may finish even on Friday at lunchtime. I wonder whether we could use the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure that we will be completing on Thursday, that we will be finished on Thursday. And on Friday, if Mr. Niemann can start with his opposite evidence, rebuttal, then that would be fine, the rebuttal on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We would certainly like to take advantage of Friday, if we could, call a witness, one witness. The only thing that concerns me is coming to some arrangement with Mr. Fila, that he has actually closed his case. We don't want to start our rebuttal evidence until he has closed. So it may be that the evidence that he still wishes to call, that he wants the day and a half for in June, is something that we can agree upon and there would be no difficulty, and if it's something that he wants to put forward. But my only concern is that I would ask that he close his case before we present our rebuttal evidence. But if he does that, then we would like to take advantage of Friday to at least call one witness. I think we have one witness we could call.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours -- well, let's make it simple. This week I am completing my evidence, so-to-speak, which are important to determine whether Dokmanovic is guilty or not. After that I have no further evidence. The evidence that I am talking about for June will be the family and friends of Dokmanovic, to give a character sketch of him, and an expert. I think we are going to have Mr. Aleksic, if I can find him, or somebody else if not, that has practised in Yugoslavia. So in practical terms on Thursday, Mr. Niemann, I am completing my Defence case. Have I made myself clearer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, wouldn't be a difficulty for us, if it's limited and restricted only to character evidence and Mr. Dokmanovic, and indeed if he wants to call some evidence about sentencing, we have no problem with that either. It's really no different than what the position was before. But we'd ask that it be restricted to that, because we don't want to have to embark upon our rebuttal case only to have it interrupted by further Defence evidence which we are going to have to then rebut again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Fila promised, that in June --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm giving you my word. If not, shall I sign my statement for Mr. Niemann? Do you want me to sign?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we may start again at 2.15? Thank you. --- Luncheon recess at 12.42 p.m. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Fila or Mr. Petrovic? Mr. Petrovic, our next witness is Mr. Susa Vojin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is Mr. Zlatic, Radoslav Zlatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, I have good news, finally, on these prints. I understand that they have been made, and so I should be able to provide those to the court in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is one of the witnesses for whom we have no witness statement. Am I correct in saying there is no witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We do have a statement, a statement had been made and it was submitted, and you will also be given one copy of the statement now, but it is a short one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's going to be very brief, Your Honour. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I ask you to read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatic, do you remember that on the 28th of January, 1998, you gave a statement to the investigator of the Fila law firm? I would kindly ask this to be shown to the witness. And if this is your statement, would you please say so?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there are no objections, I would tender this statement into evidence as a Defence exhibit, and could this please be given the next number in order together with the English translation, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Defence Exhibit 111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see there is no objection, so it is submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatic, did you complete secondary traffic school in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: I worked as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: I was employed in the Panonija Osijek company and I worked there for 21 years until the beginning of the crisis in Yugoslavia when I was evicted from Osijek, that is, I was forced to flee together with my family to Belgrade, where I was accommodated in the Kasino Hotel. This is my story.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long have you been working as a driver for the Ministry of Justice in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: When I came to Belgrade, I met Mr. Susa, and at that time he was proposed Minister of the Serbian governments, Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, and Srem, and since I had a new car, a new Zastava 128, I used to drive him to the government sessions and meetings in Erdut, and I used to drive that vehicle for about six or seven months, until it was destroyed, but I remained with Mr. Susa throughout the war and I used to work for the Ministry of Administration and Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you drove Mr. Susa in your own car, your private car?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic and how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: I've known Slavko Dokmanovic because of the sports. My village, the village of Cepin, and Trpinja used to play football together in the district of Osijek, and I used to know him and Mr. Trosic, and when the whole thing started, I used to see him on TV. And after I became a refugee, I used to see him at the meetings of the government. I was never personally introduced to him, but I used to know him by sight very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, were you in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When were you told that you would go to Vukovar on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Well, we used to meet every evening in the Kasino Hotel, me and Susa, and he told me to go to Vukovar -- that we were going to Vukovar to get some fuel because there was a shortage of fuel, and I happened to get some near the Zvezda stadium, and at 7.00 a.m., Voja arrived and we set out for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you left for Vukovar from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: We arrived in Vukovar sometime after 9.00 a.m., I don't know what exactly -- what time it was. I didn't look at my watch. The road conditions were quite bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where exactly did you arrive in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: We went to Vukovar via Sid, Banovci, Orolik, and Negoslavci, and this is the route we took to get to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you do in the compound? Where did you stop?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: We when we arrived there, we saw some soldiers at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us once again where exactly you stopped?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: We stopped at VELEPROMET, which is situated at the entrance to Vukovar, from the direction of Negoslavci, at the left side. So we introduced ourselves to the person who was at the gate, so they let us in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you were within the compound of the VELEPROMET company?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew the location from before because I used to be a driver and I used to drive goods to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did you see in the yard of VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of people there and most of them were members of the government: Mr. Susa, Mr. Vojnovic. I also saw Mr. Arkan there, Mr. Kosic, and this person -- yes, Cznevevic (phoen), he's from the area of Osijek, he used to go to school with my sister, he was Minister of Education in that government, and all members of the government were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone filming the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. These people came sometime after 12.00, maybe around 1.00 in the afternoon, there was some kind of delegation, including Slavko, who was with them, and he was filming the area with a camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At one point did members of the government withdraw from the area that they were staying and did they go to some kind of gathering?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: I met several colleagues of mine, drivers who are also from Vukovar and who used to work with me in the Panonija company. At one point I was told that they were leaving because a meeting was supposed to start, and Susa told me not to stick around, not to -- go anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long these members of the government stayed in that room?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: For about an hour maybe, an hour and a half, approximately. Mr. Susa told me that they would have some short meeting of the government to show something at the deliberation of Vukovar, and this was supposed to be held in Vukovar because they did not have any better place to hold that kind of meeting. So that was the reason why that gathering or meeting took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify. You saw someone filming the yard in VELEPROMET. I assume you didn't mean Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, it was somebody else, a plump person, same height as myself. He had some kind of green jacket on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After the gathering was finished, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: After it was finished and after they left the meeting of the government, there were a lot of people in the yard, and Voja spent some time, maybe 20 minutes or half an hour, talking to some people, and a column of vehicles had been formed in the meantime, including military trucks, and they were all civilians, nobody was wearing any kind of uniform, and they went in the direction of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In which direction did you go?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: We went, we took the same road back, via Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask that the witness be shown a videotape of the Defence marked D2, and I think the hour is 15.26, and then -- 15.36, I'm sorry, and I would then kindly ask the witness to describe the area. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is this? Could you hold on a second? Could we have the monitor be switched on for the witness, please, and could you please rewind the tape a little bit to the beginning of this particular segment? Where is this? Do you recognise this area?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the exit from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you stop the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the road towards Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are these the last houses of the town?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the next houses are where?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: In Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we go on, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: There used to be a huge hole here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we stop the tape, please? Yes. Thank you. Could you recognise this area?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Now, this is quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you go on with the tape just a little bit and slowly? In slow motion, please. If you don't recognise the area, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, it's really very difficult. All I can see is this bus here and some bushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, I mean, really, it's very difficult to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Slowly I think you will be able to recognise the next segment.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Could you stop the tape here? This is Negoslavci, I believe. This is the entrance to the village after the curve. The road from Vukovar to Negoslavci is pretty straight and then there's a curve and then it's Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you stop anywhere on the road after Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: The column was moving quite slowly, and before we entered Orolik, we stopped, and they wanted to know why we were waiting. There were some people from the Red Cross there who were distributing food to the people on the buses, some cookies, juices, and things like that, and I noticed that there was a commotion at the entrance, and I remember that there used to be a military checkpoint there, a kind of swing gate, some kind of temporary swing gate, and a soldier was there all the time. I noticed that there was a commotion there, and I wanted to see what was happening and why we were waiting. I wanted to know why civilian vehicles couldn't be let through. When I got there, I saw Mr. Dokmanovic, who was having an argument with this soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When exactly was that, what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: It was getting dark, it was at dusk. It was a nice day, a sunny day, but in the afternoon hours, fog settled in. The argument was quite heated, and I was actually surprised to see Slavko to have such an argument with a soldier. But at one point, from the house which was on the left-hand side, from the direction of Vukovar, ten soldiers appeared with automatic rifles and they cocked their rifles, and at one point I thought to myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you last see Slavko Dokmanovic on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Well, this was around 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatic, I don't know whether it was a mistake in translation or not, but did you say that Mr. Susa worked for the Justice Ministry in Belgrade? Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't say that. Mr. Susa was Minister of Justice and Administration -- that's how it was called at that time -- with the government of Western Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem. No, he didn't work for the Serbian Ministry of Justice. This does not appear in my statement and I didn't say that. I've been with this man from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I know it didn't appear in your statement. It's just that I saw that as something that was said in the transcripts. Never mind. On the day that you set off to go to VELEPROMET, how did you know that you should go there, to that particular place in Vukovar, VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Well, on the evening, Susa told me that I would be going and that there would be a session of the government in Vukovar, so I didn't have to ask where and why. As we were approaching the area, the first houses and the area near VELEPROMET, at that moment I was told that the meeting would be held there. I used to know Vukovar very well from before the war. Osijek is not very far from Vukovar. I used to work there very often, so I knew the area and I knew where VELEPROMET was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at VELEPROMET, where did you park the car?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Inside the compound. We entered the compound of VELEPROMET.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you leave the car parked in there, inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, inside the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were there for some time, from 8.00, 9.00, right through until the end of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you leave VELEPROMET at all that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. There was a kitchen there where they were distributing food and water to women and children. There was even some cooked food, beans, I think I remember they had for lunch, and there was this man who was standing outside and he was distributing food from a huge pot, and I also ate there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you didn't see vehicles or buses arriving at the JNA barracks nearby during the course of that morning?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see buses arriving in VELEPROMET itself?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time did they arrive in VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Well, they kept coming one by one, maybe two by two. They would enter the compound and the civilians were boarding buses, and there were also military lorries there. As far as I heard, there was a problem, something like Croatia did not want to receive them, to have them back, and that the area was heavily mined. This is something that I heard later on. They went via Bosanski Samac, these women and children. This took place -- this happened for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, apart from the women and children, did you see any men that had been taken prisoner, Croatian men?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were some people who were there. I mean, nobody -- as far as I could tell, nobody was captured, they were simply there, and apparently they had expressed a wish to go and they all left. There were lots of men there, elderly men, but there were more women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you see, first see Mr. Dokmanovic, about what time?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: I saw him sometime before 1.00 p.m. I really couldn't tell you the time. I never thought that I would be a witness here. This all took place a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course you can only tell us what best you can remember. Who did he arrive with? Who did Mr. Dokmanovic arrive with?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, they were waiting for him and he was supposed to arrive with a delegation from Serbia, some people who were involved in economic matters and things like that, people unknown to me. I don't know how many there were, about four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him arrive?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you didn't recognise the people he was with?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, these people were unknown to me. I had not seen them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, shortly after Mr. Dokmanovic arrived, did they then have the government meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, they withdrew to a kind of room which is on the right-hand side from the entrance to the compound. They used to have their administration there. This is where I used to report before when I would come to VELEPROMET as a driver. And this is where they went together with my Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the government delegation set off on a tour of Vukovar at any stage either before or after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: I don't think they were able to leave after the meeting. We had been there for a very short while, and it was very difficult for us. We were waiting for our turn to join the column. Later on I saw Slavko in Orolik at the checkpoint where this minor incident took place. My assumption was, my conclusion was, that he had left before us. In my opinion, there was no possibility whatsoever, no opportunity to go to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So as best you know, they simply left VELEPROMET and went out with the convoy of buses?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Dokmanovic at Orolik, did you hear him speaking? Did you hear what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes. Why they were stopping us, why they didn't want to let us go, we were in a hurry, he had some visitors from Serbia, I don't know whether they were visitors or something else, we were supposed to pass, and this person was telling us that nobody could pass before they received what they needed and -- anyway, this is what happened. And I was actually surprised at the violence of the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was being violent? Mr. Dokmanovic or the soldier or both?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Well, they were all quite violent, especially Mr. Dokmanovic. He was probably very angry because he was with that delegation, he was supposed to go somewhere, and these people were members of the government of Baranja, Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem, and soldiers wouldn't simply let anyone pass without some kind of authorisation that they were apparently waiting for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Dokmanovic say that he was a member of the government, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he said he was a member of the government --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't help. It didn't help. In the meantime, these soldiers came out from that house with their rifles cocked and I was -- I started to worry about our safety. I thought that the situation was quite serious because they were armed, they had cocked their rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many vehicles were there held up from this delegation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count them. I mean, I wasn't interested to know at the time. We were all in a hurry. You know, at that time it was still quite dangerous to drive along that road, especially during the night, because the road between Orolik and Sid, the Ustashas were still there some 200 metres away. There were daily shootings. Our soldiers were going back home and there were lots of civilians too. So it was quite dangerous for us to pass that road during the night. And we were in a hurry. We wanted to leave as soon as possible. I don't know where our people went, but we went to Sid that night, we had dinner in Sid, and then after that, we left for Belgrade. As for Slavko, I don't know where he went because -- you couldn't overtake anyone on that road. I mean, it was a very -- the road was in a very bad condition, full of holes. It was a muddy road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you manage to make it to Sid before it was dark?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, no. It was already getting dark in Orolik, and I think that we stayed there for about half an hour, even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you left VELEPROMET, did you leave at the same time as all the buses left, the buses of all the people?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: You know, not everyone can leave at the same time -- could leave at the same time, so we were waiting for our chance, our opportunity to join the column, and those who joined the column beforehand were able to leave before. There were lots of vehicles at that point. And as soon as I got my chance, I joined the column. And probably Slavko managed to get in the column before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember whether the buses that were in the convoy were ahead of you or behind you when you set off from VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Both ahead of us and behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were in the middle of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: More or less, I think. I don't know how many were behind me and how many were ahead of me, but I was a hundred metres away from the swing gate, and since a bus, I think, is maybe 10 or 12 metres long, there were maybe between 10 and 15 buses ahead of me and a couple of cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, occasionally did you and Mr. Susa stay over in Erdut, overnight in Erdut, when you were there on government business?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you stay when you had to stay overnight rather than go back to Belgrade? Where did you stay? Where were you accommodated?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: We stayed where the meeting was held. On the top floor upstairs, there were about five or six beds. Sometimes there would be no room for us to stay there, and then we would sleep at the place that before the war used to be some kind of military training centre. There were lots of beds there, and this is where we sometimes stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This military training centre was the military training centre of Mr. Arkan's people, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: It's kind of pre-military. It was used for that purpose before the war, and I don't know what purpose it served afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before the war, you mean before --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the war, when I used to have that kind of training, pre-army training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But at the time that you stayed there with Mr. Susa, when you used to stay in the dormitories, that was then a training centre for Mr. Arkan's people, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is where they used to sleep, live, and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any connection that you could see between the government, the government of the Serbian district, and Mr. Arkan's military people? I mean, you stayed in their dormitories, but was there any other connection that you observed?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sure. What I'm asking you is whether you saw any connection between the government that Mr. Susa was the Minister of Justice for and Mr. Arkan's military group that was located at these dormitories where you used to sleep occasionally?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just two short questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Susa had left the room where the meeting was held, did you hang around in the VELEPROMET yard for a while?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, we stayed there for a while. He discussed things with certain people, I had started the engine, and I was waiting for my turn to leave the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But did you see Slavko Dokmanovic leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. We were the first ones to arrive, Voja and myself, so I was parked, I was stationed next to the gate, so I could see everyone entering and leaving the VELEPROMET compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you see him leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV ZLATIC
utterances.text: He was sitting on the right side next to the driver, front passenger seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume there is no objection to the witness being released? Mr. Zlatic, thank you for testifying in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I be excused for the rest of the afternoon? I have a commitment in another Chamber. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, did you make a statement to Mr. Vasic on the 14th of August -- no, on the 30th of September, '97? Will you take a look at the document and tell us whether that is your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is document D112 and D112A for the translation.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is my statement and my signature on the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, I tender this into evidence as D112 and D112A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, did you graduate from the faculty of law and when?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I graduated from the faculty of law at the faculty in Osijek and I graduated in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you, in your later career, were you the Public -- the Prosecutor in Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, between 1983 and 1990, I was the deputy of the district, Public Prosecutor, and I was also the Public Prosecutor later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long did you perform that function, until what time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Until February 1991, and officially right up to September of the same year when I was relieved of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why were you relieved of your duties?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I was relieved of my duties due to the fact that I had to -- I was forced to leave the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to leave the Republic of Croatia? Were you arrested or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: As I say, in February 1991, I was subjected to an operation, a gallbladder operation, and after that operation, I spent time recuperating at home, and on the 9th of July, 1991, within my family circle, by a special unit of the Zengara, I was arrested, and I was taken to a camp, collection camp, which was improvised at the stadium of the football club of Zupanja and Vinkovci. I had a lot of trouble there, I was maltreated, and I was physically injured, and on the following day, in a state of that kind, I was allowed to leave the town towards Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Physical mistreatment meant you had injuries, did it not?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I sustained injuries of the mouth because a rifle was introduced into my mouth and it went right up to the right sinus channel, I lost two teeth on the occasion, and two ribs were broken on the right-hand side. I had a dislocated shoulder and had to be treated for those injuries at the emergency centre in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did they do this to you? Why did you sustain these injuries?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Because the group came to our house, as I say, and my father was arrested on the occasion, and they allegedly stated that we lent our support to the insurgence in Mirkovci, it is a village near Vinkovci, and allegedly on that night there was shooting from our house in the direction of the Zengara patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that of course was not true?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I met Slavko Dokmanovic for the first time on the 18th of August, 1991, at a meeting which was held in Dalj when we discussed the need to constitute an organ which should represent the government and when for Mr. Dokmanovic -- when it was stated that he was a pretender for the function of Agriculture Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you elected as Minister of Justice and Administration in the government and how were you elected?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I was elected to that function at the proposal of Goran Hadzic. I was nominated by the Great National Assembly of the Srem district of the day, Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who represented that Assembly and how were you elected?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The Assembly was represented by the deputies who, in fact, physically represented the people from the locality in such a way as in the composition of the Great National Assembly, all those were entered who at the previous elections in Croatia got the vote of the people as well as the representatives of the villages from which these people were not formally elected at the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does this refer to the elections in 1990, the first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, the elections held in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should like now to show the witness some documents that have already been accepted as Exhibits D59 -- D16 and D59, I think. D59, please, Exhibit D59.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is the decision on the election of the President or Vice-President, Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister of the government of the Serbian -- district of Serbia, Baranja, and Western Srem, on the basis of -- who wrote this decision and what was it based on?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The decision was written by an expert service, a professional service, that is to say the secretariat of the Great National Assembly, and noting this conclusion, I took part, I gave certain suggestions as to how it should be shaped and the formal wording, and it was adopted at the Great National Assembly, the date is stated, it is the 25th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is the exact date and it enumerates all the Ministers who were elected, amongst them yourself and Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we now have Exhibit D60, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is the law governing Ministries. Would you look and tell us who wrote the law?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The law was devised in my Ministry by my associates, Mr. Milos Vojnovic and the late Mr. Nenad Stankovic. I myself took part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you take a look at item 10, please? It is the article which relates to the Ministry of Agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture was Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell me the competencies of his activities?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In order to explain what his functions were, I should have to elaborate the meaning of an administration, administrative rule for the state to become a state and a region, and I must say that in that sense, Mr. Dokmanovic fulfilled his duties correctly. Therefore, first of all, he organised work on the farming collectives for the area in which we lived and the area that we controlled and he performed all the functions that meant cooperation with organisations which we did not have on the spot at the time and which dealt with the processing of farming goods so as to ensure their functioning and supplies, food supplies for the population of the area, and I must stress, which the court already knows, I'm sure, that the area we lived in was one of the best farming areas in the former Yugoslavia, agricultural areas, and therefore Mr. Dokmanovic's job was highly responsible and a highly difficult job to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we show the witness Exhibit D19 now, please?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: That is the law on Territorial Defence, Territorial organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that also a law which was written in your Ministry?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you took part in its elaboration?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A question was raised with the Territorial organisation as to why we have municipalities which were not within your realm, for example, the Municipality of Osijek, the inhabited region of Osijek. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, let me say that we had many people working in our various organs, bodies, who came from urban areas, from towns bordering upon us, that is to say Osijek and Vinkovci, and those individuals insisted that those two towns be incorporated into the law on Territorial organisation as something which we, at a given moment, can count on, although it was certain that at that time we were not controlling those two towns and that it was a debatable point whether we would ever succeed in controlling them. Let me stress, for example, with the example of Osijek, that a section of the town, the lower town, as it was called, was inhabited by mostly Serbs who were expelled from the area. And that according to the population census of 1991, done by the organs of Croatia, that this was ascertained in that census. So what was written was purely symbolic, which for a very brief period of time was put down on paper, whereas several months later, after we had written this down, the Municipalities of Prenj (sic) and Mirkovci was set up, which means that this symbolism ceased to exist after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How was the territory, local self government organised?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The Territorial organisation was organised in pyramid form with regard to the conditions that prevailed. At the bottom, at the base, were the local communities. Above them, we had the municipalities, the communes, and then the government as executive power and authority which functioned. Then you had the legislative authorities represented by the Great National Assembly and Independent Court rule at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, how did this Territorial organisation function at that level until the constitutional law was enacted; that is, since the adoption of the constitutional law?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, before that, there were elections which were held, and after the constitutional law was enacted, I must stress with provisional meaning, until we were able to organise elections, which, due to the conflicts that lasted, that was not possible. We organised this in such a way as having the locals of individual villages elected their representatives. The number depended on the size of the particular locality and number of settlements in it. These representatives, furthermore, through meetings and joint decisions, decided, together with the government, as to who would be their representative for the municipality, and then from the municipalities, the representatives would be delegated once again, depending on the number of inhabitants, into the Great National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that is why it is called the law on the provisional, the word is "provisional"?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, we bore this in mind because it was truly provisional for anything to be able to function and to establish administrative rule in any way until democratic free elections could be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And finally to conclude this, how did the system of authority function, of government function?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, due to the prevailing conditions, there was still armed -- there was still armed combat on both sides, it was difficult for us to establish the necessary discipline on this part and all this functioned very badly, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the composition of your government, did you have the Ministries for the army, the police, and did you have armed forces and a police force, particularly in November 1991, because that is the subject of our interests?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I must say that when we enacted these provisions, we sort of looked towards the future at a time when this would be necessary and would be able to function. That is why formally we did have an Internal Affairs Ministry and a Defence Ministry formally. But, unfortunately, these Ministers did not have anything much to do because neither did they have a police force which could function on the spot nor could the Defence Minister bring in any decisions because, behind him or below him, he had nobody, that is to say, he had no armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the next document that we're going to show you and tell us what it purports to? May we have a number for those exhibits, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is document D113.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have in mind the decision to conjoin the annexation of the territory, so three decisions.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I recall one particular meeting that I attended when we discussed the fact that we had a lot of problems with the armed formations which existed at the level of every inhabited region and which had no unified command. We did not have an organ which would be able to control it, and this was necessary. First of all, because of the pilfering and looting that was taking place and it was logical, and I think that Mr. Koncarevic decided this with the military authorities, that everybody carrying weapons in our area without a uniform command be placed under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have in mind the village watches?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. We only had in mind the village watches because we had nobody else carrying weapons in an organised fashion. Had it been organised, we would have stood up against it and coming under the JNA with which we did not particularly cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The date this decision was made was the 9th of October, 1990 -- was it 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The 10th of October is the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There must be an error. Does that mean that after the 10th of October, the village watches had nothing to do with you? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, this need not be true in absolute terms because the village watches always found ways of retaining their autonomy with the local commanders, but this was not a problem that we were supposed to deal with but it was now a problem of the JNA. But up till then, the local commanders, or the commanders of the village watches, found ways and means of cooperating with officers covering that particular territory so that together, strengthened by the arms they had, would enter into looting and pilfering and doing a lot of valuable stealing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's clear up the matter of the relationship between your government and the JNA. What kind of relationship did you have?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: It wasn't a good relationship because the Yugoslav People's Army did not consider us to be a serious partner, not only in military matters, which might have been true, but also in the sense of establishing administrative civilian rule which we insisted upon and which did not -- they did not agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any possibility of ordering the JNA anything, demanding that they perform anything?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, we had to seek ways and means, each of us, as best we could, to use our friendship with somebody to be able to get something done, which was necessary to be able to bring life to a semblance of normality, but we did not have the possibility of calling upon one of the senior commanders and demand that something be done. That was never the case. We could never do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So could I then conclude that no military forces -- that you were not an authority for any of them?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you, on the 20th of November, 1991, go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you arrive? Where did you arrive from and why did you go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
