utterances.text: As I said, I provisionally -- temporarily lived in Belgrade, and the way in which I functioned was that I would travel from Belgrade towards Erdut, and that's what I did on that particular day. I left from Belgrade, but not in the direction of Erdut but in the direction of Vukovar. On the previous day, that is to say the 19th, I was in Erdut, which is where the government was stationed, and Mr. Goran Hadzic informed us on the occasion that he had had talks with his associates who had returned from the terrain and that he was told that in the course of the following day, operations would be completed for the liberation, as we called it, the liberation of Vukovar, and that it would be a good idea, in view of our importance, which was not very great, but due to the fact that we wanted to establish quite different forms of cooperation with the Yugoslav People's Army that, on the following day, we should meet in Vukovar so as to agree upon what should be done to establish administrative civilian structures in the town and to see what the town looks like after the very long and terrible bombing that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should like the witness now to be shown the minutes, but the minutes are in Belgrade. So can I show him my copy? I think that the Prosecutor's office will be able to ascertain that it is the same document. If that is possible. It is Defence Exhibit D53, the original of which is in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that the minutes of the meeting held in Erdut on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Those are the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you like to comment? You are a lawyer, a legal man. How were these meetings held from the legal aspect?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The government meetings were held very regularly. As far as the government was concerned, we had the responsibility ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ah, we found a copy, a court copy. It's the same document.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, the members of the government had agreed not to improvise, not to take up each other's time, so we would prepare in writing all the proposals for the meetings and the conclusions of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the agenda as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. It was always the responsibility of the government secretariat to set up an agenda, to write down an agenda. Sometimes we had problems with this because some of the Ministers wanted to introduce items on the agenda which had not been previously written down, and we thought that we should only answer their needs sometimes when it was an urgent matter but not as standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the government meetings, was a quorum determined?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. No decision could be endorsed at the Great National Assembly if the proposal for a decision was made at a government meeting without a quorum.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do you mean by quorum? Fifty plus one?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, when the government takes decisions. This is so in all the systems that we have had occasion to acquaint ourselves with, the government takes a decision as a proposal for the Great National Assembly with a majority which is represented by the 50 plus one system.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the minutes that you have, was that enacted in the same way?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were government decisions always verified by the Great National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, that was an obligation. They were always verified by the Great National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to tell us, if you will, something about some of the points in the document that we're interested in. Look at page 2, please, and item by item tell us what it represents. What does item 1 mean, that "Caslav Ocic," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: That is clear. If the town has been liberated, we knew that in the town there were a large number of civilians and soldiers, regardless of whether they were Serbs or Croats, Caslav Ocic and Mr. Ilija Petrovic, who likes literary forms of expression, were to prepare a proclamation for the citizens of Vukovar calling upon people to respect law and order and to establish those basic elements of law and order, which would encourage people after everything that had taken place. Mr. Caslav Ocic was to have, under item 2, prepared information about the government's views to send the blue helmets --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's finish with item 1, please. Was it determined when the proclamation would be given and was it to have been verified previously by the government? What does the word "preparation" mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, everything that had a deadline was to have been expressed in writing. Therefore, Mr. Ocic and Ilija Petrovic were clearly in principle in keeping with the possibilities and the time they have at their disposal, and in view of all the foregoing events, would prepare a proclamation for the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And were you to verify that proclamation as the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they do that by the following day?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us now go on to item 2, that Caslav Ocic prepares information, what information?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: At that time we discussed the need to send neutral forces of a third party to the area, and we, that is not myself but I think it was Goran Hadzic, had had preliminary talks for the establishment of a UN mission in the locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To what aim?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: First of all, to stabilise the region and to prevent any further conflicts from breaking out because we assessed that any war which would be prolonged, we would not be able to contend with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we now go on to item 3? What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I have already mentioned that our work so far, in cooperation with the members of the JNA, was at a very low level. Most of the time we said things to each other, we would agree upon certain things, but nothing was ever implemented on the ground. There were people within the government who were close to some of the members -- some of the representatives of the Republic of Serbia and who believed that, through their mediation, a new course would set in within the JNA and that it would be allowed for the people in that area to organise themselves independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that until the 19th, the situation was not that way, it was not the case, before and after? When was the first time you established civilian authority, first attempted and then succeeded in doing so?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I think that after the liberation of Vukovar, maybe a month, month and a half after the liberation, some kind of executive government was established through the executive council which was at that time presided by Mr. Rajko Bibic, until that time we had some kind of military rule that was represented by members of the Yugoslav People's Army, and before that, we had a very, very poor plan at that time for the -- for the town of Ilok, which was completely under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that? Neither before the 19th nor after the 19th there was no cooperation with the representatives of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. I said that neither after the 19th was there any cooperation and nor was it the case before the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to speak slowly so that we can have everything in the transcript. I would now kindly ask you to give us some explanation as to item 5. I don't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Item 5 expresses a wish, a need, which unfortunately until that time or after that time was brought to life, implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now, please have a look at the item 3 which says that Goran Hadzic -- item 3 and under item 3, Goran Hadzic hereby informs members of the government and so on. Could you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: This was more like an invitation for us to meet in Vukovar on the next day, which was perfectly clear to most of the members of the government. They were people from Vukovar and they could hardly wait for the first possibility, first opportunity to go to Vukovar to see their houses, their friends, and I was interested in that too, although I'm not from Vukovar, but I wanted to attend, to be present at that event, which was supposed to be of a ceremonial character.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you can see, a distinction is being made here between the need for government members to be in Vukovar on Wednesday and the session of the government which is convened on the 22nd in Beli Manastir. Are these two separate things?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, they are. You can see it from the text. On the 22nd of November, a regular session of the government was held, according to the procedure which I have described. Everybody had prepared a report on the activities, and this was not something that was supposed to be done in Vukovar. I think that at that time we assumed, we had some kind of idea of the situation we would find in Vukovar, and nobody thought that anything seriously could be done in Vukovar in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, would you agree with me that whatever was held in Vukovar on the 20th was not a meeting of the government? It was not a session of the government.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: It was not a session of the government but it was a meeting of the members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether the majority of government members were present?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Not all of them were there but the majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us see now. When did you arrive in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I believe that we arrived in Vukovar from Belgrade around half past ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The reason for your visit to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: We wanted to be there, to gather there. In VELEPROMET, the so-called VELEPROMET compound, around 12.00. That's what Goran Hadzic said. And he knew that we were supposed to come from different points, but anyway, we were supposed to meet at 12.00 at the VELEPROMET building.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At what time did you enter the VELEPROMET compound?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I arrived in Vukovar around 10.30 and I couldn't resist the proposal of one of our colleagues who had joined us on our trip from Belgrade to Vukovar and who insisted that we should go and see what was left of his house. Unfortunately, nothing was left of his house, but we were supposed to move around very carefully because the town was in a horrible state and at certain points we had to bypass a number of dead bodies who were still lying around. We had to go over some destruction, smithereens, and we also had to cover the area which was probably mined. But although we were aware of that, we wanted to follow him, we wanted to escort him, so we reached his house and we stayed there for a while. He was very distressed. The name of this person is Nikola Drpa. And after that, we went back to VELEPROMET via the same way, and I think we arrived there at about ten, quarter to twelve.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At what time did you see Slavko Dokmanovic, if you did see him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I saw Slavko Dokmanovic when I got to the yard, to the compound of VELEPROMET, and he was accompanied by some people whom I had not seen before. These people were not members of the government, but I didn't know whether they were from Vukovar because I didn't live in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So did Slavko Dokmanovic attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he present there all the time, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I think he was present there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any agenda on that meeting? Were minutes taken during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, we thought that the meeting would be held in a much better atmosphere, and we hoped that there would be room for us for some kind of satisfaction, but the town itself and the people we found there, especially the victims that were there, made us feel really aghast at what we saw. We were really terribly depressed with what we saw in the town and the people we ran into. So nobody -- no member of the government began the meeting. It was some kind of low-ranking officer, maybe Lieutenant Colonel, and I believe his surname was Vojnovic, he was given to us to open the meeting. So he formally chaired the meeting. He was sitting at the table, or maybe he was standing next to the table in front of us, and we were sitting like this, the way I am sitting now facing you here in the courtroom. So we were sitting in rows of tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good time for a break or maybe -- do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. A 20-minute break?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All rise. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like the tape, Defence Exhibit No. 2 be shown to the witness. The time is 15.50, VELEPROMET. I would like to ask him whether he was there, whether he recognises some people on the video. A very brief segment of the tape. If you see Slavko Dokmanovic, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who else can you see?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I can see Rade Leskovac, Vlado Kosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this the time prior to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. This is Goran Hadzic and Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan. This is Ljubo Mudrinic, Slavko Dokmanovic, Dusan Jaksic, Vlado Kosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That would be enough. Mr. Susa, do you recognize this as the day when you went to Vukovar, the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that I saw on the tape tells me that this is the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you want to see some more of the tape or are you sure that this was the situation on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure, the way people looked and because I saw them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that the meeting was convened for 12.00. Now you can see that it's past 1.00 and the meeting has not started yet. When did it start?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, we were supposed to gather at the VELEPROMET building around noon and the meeting started rather late because we were waiting for Mr. Hadzic. And then when he arrived, the meeting didn't start right away because we were waiting for someone to let us into the building of VELEPROMET. So this lasted until 14.00, 2.00, when this gentleman appeared, I think it was this lieutenant-colonel by the name of Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you remember the contents of the meeting --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise. But can this monitor be turned off? I cannot concentrate myself very well. Excuse me, could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you entered the room where the meeting was held, you said before the break how the seating arrangements looked like. Could you tell us who sat where?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, we were not put in line. We simply entered the room and he sat next to the desk. He was standing next to the table and then we sat on the benches, which were arranged in school-like manner. Mr. Hadzic was sitting in the first row, Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan was also there, and I was sitting maybe also in the first row but to the right-hand side. People sat down without any particular order. They simply took the seats that were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could we say that he was sitting like some kind of teacher, and would you agree with us that he conducted the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, and without his approval it was impossible for us to enter the room. And that's what he said. He said that he had some time and that he was able to talk to us, and if we had any kind of proposal or suggestions, that he was willing to listen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Some people who thought they knew something about the military doctrine and who did describe -- who did say that the manner in which Vukovar was liberated was not very good, had an opportunity to confirm that, and to say it publicly. I'm not sure, but I believe that Mr. Pajo Nedic was objecting to the shelling of Vukovar and the way it was conducted, because the town was reduced to rubble. And for the people who are from Vukovar, were very hurt by what they said. And I can tell you for myself, after I had seen what the situation was, I was also concerned. Dr. Hadzic also talked, and he was really distressed with what he had seen, and he spoke in some general terms about the need to repair the town so that people would be able to live normally in that town. Dokmanovic also spoke. He addressed the need to organise as soon as possible, together with the army and the people in general, to organise harvest and preparations that were necessary for the sowing. I also mentioned this when I discussed with the members of the Prosecution, and this is the impression that I had. This speech that was made by Dokmanovic seem to me quite strange, bizarre, almost surreal, in view of what was going on around us. However, I can very well understand that at that time his attitude was very professional and he was perfectly conscious that without agriculture, which was the basis for life in the area, that without agriculture we would never be able to repair the town and to enable its population to live normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you sure that Pajo Nedic was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I already told you that I'm not sure that that was Pajo Nedic. Somebody spoke, several people spoke, but someone was very insistent, and he said, Mr. Vojnovic, that the army, in that action, in that operation, which had lasted for several months, had done -- excuse my language -- had done a shitty business. Mr. Vojnovic had nothing to say in that sense. He said that that was the strategy, that was the doctrine that they had adopted and had resulted in the not very large number of casualties. And I think he had the JNA in mind when he said that. And he said that a grave number of people was supposed to find accommodation as soon as possible, because people kept pouring out of the shelters, out of the basements and the town. There were Croats there, Serbs, people who had been fortunate enough to survive what was happening in the town. And I'm not talking only about the operations carried out by the JNA. There were lots of internal settling of accounts. There were lots of people who had acted on their own, who had established their own groups, and I am referring to parts of Croatian formations, and who were terrorising the population in the town. And the corpses that I saw in the streets were not the corpses of Croats or Serbs. They were corpses of some people who happened to be there and they were all mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that the meeting lasted for about one hour. Where did you go after the meeting? Did you stay for a while at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I stayed in the yard, the VELEPROMET compound, and most of the people who had been at the meeting stayed there, remained there for a while, because they were waiting in line to get out of the VELEPROMET compound. Some sort of traffic jam had been created there. There was a great number of vehicles in the street in front of the VELEPROMET compound. There was no order whatsoever at that moment, and we were in a great hurry, and half an hour later we managed to join the convoy that was headed no Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, did you see when Slavko Dokmanovic left? Did he leave before you or later on?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I did not pay attention to Slavko Dokmanovic at that moment, and I don't know whether he had left before me, but if you want me, I can add. Later on I saw him ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you see him? You saw him after the meeting and did after 3 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, the meeting ended around 3.00. I cannot tell you the exact time, and I wouldn't commit myself in that way, but the first time that I saw him after the meeting, it was before the village of Orolik, and it was the last time I saw him on that day. And I didn't see him again before several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened in Orolik?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The convoy vehicles stopped before Orolik, including my vehicle. At that moment I didn't see anything, however, my driver noticed that something was happening ahead of us, some kind of incident is taking place, and threatened to become a real conflict with casualties maybe. And when my driver said that, he mentioned Slavko Dokmanovic, and he said that he had some kind of argument with the checkpoint control -- checkpoint patrol and that they were likely to come to blows. So he left the vehicle, he got out of the vehicle, and I got out of the vehicle after him. And at that point I saw Mr. Dokmanovic, together with Rade Leskovac, and a number of other people unknown who were to me. And I saw a number of military policemen who were quite aggressive, I assume, because they were drunk, and who had their rifles pointed towards Dokmanovic and these other people. And I believe that Mr. Leskovac acted in an inadequate manner during that incident. I believe that he was standing behind Mr. Dokmanovic and he was sort of pushing him towards these people with whom no agreement could be reached. We were simply -- we had to withdraw, simply, and this is what I suggested to Mr. Dokmanovic. But then an officer appeared, an army officer, and he ordered that the road should be cleared and that the convoy should be allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you be more specific as to the time of the day?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, that day was quite sunny, but it ended with some kind of mist. And when I saw Mr. Dokmanovic, at that point the sun had already settled down, but I think you can say that it was already dusk. After we had passed Orolik and when we reached Banovci, which is the following village, and which is maybe four or five kilometres away from Orolik, I remember that we already had our lights on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't assume you can remember the exact time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, I presume it could have been around 5.00 p.m., maybe some minutes, several minutes before that or after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And my last question. Do you remember what Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic had an uniform on, which was different from my uniform and from other similar uniforms that we were wearing. His uniform resembled the uniform that I was using before the war for hunting. It was a two-piece hunting uniform and I believe that he had the same kind of vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The one with front pockets for ammunition?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the kind of vest I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Susa, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Susa. Do you recall giving a statement to Mr. Waespi in Belgrade on the 10th and 11th of January of this year?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was that statement taken down in the English language and subsequently read back to you in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And then did you sign the statement as being true and correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. At this time I would like for you to look at this. I'll mark this as Prosecutor's Exhibit, I believe it's 206. And this statement was taken in Mr. Fila's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In a way, yes. The first day we were in the building of the Federal Executive Council and then on the second day in Mr. Fila's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you recognize your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not the same as last time. Mr. Waespi gave us that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: On all the pages of this document, which you have given me, I recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 206.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, when was the government of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem formed, initially?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The first talks about a government began at the beginning of August 1991, and at that time I was still in Belgrade for treatment. A more serious meeting on that topic was held on the 18th of August, the same year, and the government was actually constituted in September of that same year, before the Great National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So the government that was constituted in September and which we have seen a little earlier, where the ministers are set out in this document, that was the first constituting of a government, is that correct, with actual ministers?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And during the period between September and December, did the persons who were holding these ministerial posts change, or did they remain the same?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I think that during that particular period we only had one situation in which we had a change, and that was after Mr. Ilija Koic was injured, and he was Defence Minister and was replaced by his deputy, Mr. Pedra Grablovic (phoen).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How was Mr. Koic, the Defence Minister, injured? What were the circumstances under which he was injured?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was going from -- by car from Vukovar towards the village where the -- inhabited by Serbs and was then attacked from an ambush. And that particular vehicle was hit by one of these Zolja, rocket launchers, and he was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you have a Deputy Minister of Justice?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I had a deputy and several assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How many assistant ministers altogether, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, of course. I had three assistants. I don't count my deputy. I know that it was his function to help me most directly and to take my place when I was not there. Then we had the secretary in the ministry who dealt with all personnel problems and prepared and organised work within the ministry, and of course there were assistants for justice, for administration and for criminal sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was this true of the other ministries within the government as well, that there were deputy ministers and assistant ministers for the various offices?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I must say that a number of ministers did not have conditions in which they could have the luxury of deputies, so usually they nominated assistants. Some of them did have deputies, others only had assistants, because deputies were a luxury at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recall what was the situation with Mr. Dokmanovic within the Ministry of Agriculture. Did he have a deputy, assistants? How many people did he have on his staff, if any?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I can't quite remember the exact organisation as to personnel, Mr. Dokmanovic's staff, but he had several professionals working with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, do you know what the Serb National Council was? What was this organisation?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: It was an organisation, and I know as much as I've already said about it. It was organised, set up by prominent Serbs on the territory of Croatia and some other individuals who lived in Serbia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, and even in Germany, Sweden and Holland. There were about 60 odd people in the Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And the original Council was created in Serb, near Knin, in July of 1990, correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Let me say that at the time I was politically unengaged on the Serbian question side, because I performed my duties as deputy -- as public attorney in Croatia, District Attorney in Croatia. So I'm not quite sure when the Serb National Council was set up and who set it up, because several people had said that they had made the vital contribution to its founding, but I think the date that you have mentioned was generally accepted as the date when the Council was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And I was mentioning the Serb National Council from Serb, from Knin. Later on a separate Council was formed for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, was it not? If you know.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, but I did not take part in the work of either Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did the Serb National Council have a role in the formation of the governmental bodies in the Serbian district of Slovenia, Baranja and Western Srem? Did they have any part in the forming of the national assembly and the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In a way it did, yes, because it gave -- presented the idea as to how matters should be organised. The Serbian National Council did not function as an integral, organised body, but it was individuals who presented themselves as members of the Serb National Council and they were the promoters of an idea on the need to create an organ, a body which would organise and control the administration and life in a given locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that they were more of an advisory body that helped create the ideas by which the government was formed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Then you had a large role in actually the drafting of the legislation and some of the rules that we have seen by which the government operated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In a certain sense, yes, I gave some initiatives and concrete proposals which were definitely given shape to and adopted to at the Great National Assembly. Let me also tell you that I also had very many critics at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But generally the government was formed in a very organised fashion and there were clearly delineated roles for the different posts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the relationship between the government and the Serbian district -- of the Serbian District and the government of the Republic of Croatia, if any? Were there any contacts between the two?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: At that time there were no contacts, not good contacts, but no contacts. When we in mid-1992 appeared with the wish to have the most direct possible contacts with the Croatian government, a group of individuals, including myself, was politically -- fared badly politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But that was much later on; you said in 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, that was after the unification of the three Serbian districts into one whole, one entity, one organisation, which was called Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, during this period of 1991, when the conflict was going on, did your government abide by any decisions which were taken by the Croatian government in respect to the region under your control?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, we did not abide by those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And I take it there was no way for the Croatian government to enforce decisions in the area that was under your control?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In the period that you are discussing, there was no possibility for those decisions to be enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, as the battle was going on around Vukovar, the government, as I understand it, was meeting regularly in Erdut; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were meetings taking place anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: They were taking place in two localities, either in Beli Manastir or in Erdut. I don't remember exactly. It is possible that one was held in Ilok, but I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did meetings alternate between the two, for example, one meeting in Erdut, then a meeting in Beli Manastir, and the next one in Erdut, or was it more irregular?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, we could not alternate, but some people wanted to have this sort of symbolic equality between Slavonia and Srem on the one side, and Baranja on the other. However, there were areas which were physically divided, and it was really very complicated to travel such a long way, to hold meetings alternately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And how often were the meetings occurring?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: For the most part, once a week, sometimes more frequently, sometimes less frequently. In view of the problems that we discussed, and if there was the Great National Assembly before that, then we would meet twice a week, but usually it was once every two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated to Mr. Waespi in the statement that you gave to him that it was normal for local military commanders to come and give reports to the government, was it not?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but not for everyone. There were military commanders who were highly disciplined in organising the defence of their villages and they remained. And they cooperated with the government in the sense that they came to Erdut regularly and informed us as to the situation in their village. And the situation was very bad, if for nothing else, for health reasons, because we did not have the necessary health care necessary and medical aids for diseases, particularly Trichinella spiralis, the disease that was prevalent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you say they came to Erdut, would they actually attend the meetings of the government itself and brief the members as to what was going on in their areas?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The principle was that these people would inform one of the department ministers and if that minister considers it necessary to tell the other members of the government, then they would discuss the issue. Very frequently they would sit at the meetings and listen to what was going on, and we wanted to ensure the presence of the public at our meetings, because when they would go back to their own villages, they would inform the inhabitants of what we were discussing and what we were preparing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And, as I understand it, the -- these military leaders would come to you because they were having some manpower shortages as well, and were asking to you shift people who were involved in agriculture or industrial production to perform military functions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In individual villages, in some of the villages, the danger of conflicts with the opposite side was acute, and it was daily, a daily threat. And in some of the villages, such as Mirkovci, Karadzicevo, Tenia along the border-line, people would die daily. There were less and less people and we had to ensure that people -- safety for people who remained in their houses, adamant in defending them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You had also indicated to Mr. Waespi that the local commanders had in fact two superiors, the JNA who would supply them with food, weapons and wages on one hand and local civil authorities on the other hand. "When they were not able to come to terms with their military superiors, they would turn to us to complain about their problems." Just for your reference, Your Honours, I am on page 4 in the middle paragraph. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember what I told Mr. Waespi. What I said is true, but we should have an exact interpretation of the phases in which they would come to us and what they asked to us do. They never asked us concrete solutions, because they knew that we, unfortunately, did not have them at hand. But they asked us to act as arbiters in their relationship with the representatives of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So the Territorial Defence saw you as someone who can mediate between them and the JNA, and to help them solve some of their problems?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Part of the military commanders considered this. Some of us (sic) never asked us for anything. They didn't need us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you have looked at a document earlier, which I think has been entered as Defence Exhibit 113, which was the decision to attach the Territorial Defence of the Serbian district of Slovenia, Baranja and Western Srem to the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. When it refers to the Territorial Defence of the Serbian district, what does this mean? Was there an unified command or is this just talking about all of the various TO units from the different villages? Can you clarify that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I think I can tell you quite simply. Unfortunately, there was nothing that was so well organised as to represent a whole uniform command. They were -- there were village guard, watches set up earlier, which armed themselves during that period, and depending on the size of the village, and the structure of the people who imposed themselves as commanding, how that Territorial Defence would function. Sometimes, unfortunately, that Territorial Defence would mistreat the villagers in the given villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did the Minister of Defence, Mr. Koic have, in coordinating the activities of these various Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Just one correction. It was Mr. Ilija Koic. He had a very difficult task and I would say unsuccessful to the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when this decision was reached wherein the Territorial Defences were shifted over to the JNA, how was this communicated to the various Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Perhaps by means of the public information media. I don't know whether at the Ministry of Defence there were any notes written to the villages. I think that it was the radio, press and television which announced that a decision of this kind had been taken, and I suppose that later on people from the JNA began to disarm and to subject these units to themselves, who until then were in command of themselves. Their own commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated during your examination in chief that Mr. Koncarevic, I believe Ilija Koncarevic, had decided with the military authorities that everybody carrying weapons would be under the command of the JNA? Why was Mr. Koncarevic designated to carry out this discussion with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, they were very difficult talks for two reasons. First of all, there was the question of whether the army would agree for us to bring in -- bring order into such a disorganised formation, which I suppose would be a very difficult task, a thankless task. On the other hand, we had to explain to the people why they would be commanded by somebody from the JNA in future. Mr. Ilija Koncarevic, in his previous life, was an active officer of the JNA. He had some good connections there, good friends there, and by virtue of his function he was prisoned (sic) the Great National Assembly, therefore, for a political decision of this kind, a lot of strength and authority was needed so that by virtue of his function and the manner in which he was able to perform this, that was the job for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, in the meeting on the 19th of November, which occurred in Erdut, do you recall if anything else was discussed other than those items that appear in the minutes of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, all the topics -- I can't recall all the subjects in the minutes, had my attention not been drawn to them. I know that the dominant discussion was about Vukovar and about everything that we came to learn of and which indicated that a great tragedy had taken place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you indicated that Mr. Hadzic, Goran Hadzic, had been told that military options would be concluded the following day. Do you recall who had told him this, or where he learned this information?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, I don't. I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And in the minutes, and I know you may not have them in front of you any more, but it indicates that it was necessary for members of the government to be in Vukovar. This seems a little more forceful than just an invitation to attend. It's more of an indication that everyone is expected to be there; is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. You are not reading correctly, it was not stated that it was their duty to be in Vukovar. That is not stated anywhere. So if we supply you with the defence exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It appears on the English translation and that's how it appears on the transcript, that it was necessary for members of the government to be there. I've quoted it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You didn't say duty, you said necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Necessary and indispensable. It says "necessary" in the minutes and "indispensable" is something else again. Necessary, you can and you needn't. Indispensable is you must.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll read my question again. I said: It indicates that it was necessary for members of the government to be in Vukovar. This seems a little more forceful than just an invitation to attend. I quoted it verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's make one thing clear. The original exists. Would you please read it and have it translated exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think Mr. Williamson is reading from the transcript of this afternoon's hearing. So this is what the witness said before. It was necessary. So I think it is quite proper for Mr. Williamson to ask this question. So the objection is overruled. Please -- you may proceed, Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So again I would just ask you, Mr. Susa, where it indicates that it was necessary for members of the government to be in Vukovar, this seems to be a little more forceful than just an invitation. Again, it seems to be implying that there is some obligation for you to be present, or an expectation that people be present. Wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Expectation, yes, perhaps, in a way. All of us wanted to see the town, but I must tell you that when Goran Hadzic tells somebody that something would be necessary, very often this is not binding upon anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when you reached Vukovar, you indicated that you got there originally around 10.30 in the morning and went with this friend to see his house and then returned to VELEPROMET. What was the situation in VELEPROMET when you arrived back there? What did you observe going on?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: There was a lot of confusion everywhere. Everything was at the level of a catasic (phoen) day. Houses were still on fire. There was a multitude of people. Everybody was going to and fro, or at least I had that feeling, and everything gave me the picture of complete confusion. Immediately after the end of the meeting I had a strong migraine headache. There were people moving about in military uniform. There were women, men in civilian clothing. There were people crying. There were people laughing, and this all -- it seemed like a big painting of Hieronymus Bosch. That's what I said on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that those events left quite a lasting impression on you?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, they did on me, a very lasting impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when this meeting started in -- at VELEPROMET, where exactly was it held?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I did not know VELEPROMET well enough. I don't even know it now. I don't know whether I visited perhaps once or twice afterwards. But the entrance is -- you go through one entrance, one doorway, and then there is a corridor with another door and there is a room which has just that one entrance, which is both the entrance and the exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And approximately how many people were present for the meeting altogether?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: About 25 to 30 people, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recall which ministers were there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: More or less, yes. Do you want me to enumerate them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, if you can. The ones that you remember being present, by their name and their post, if possible.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: There was Goran Hadzic, who was the Prime Minister; Dr. Mladen Hadzic, who is no relation to the first, he performed the function of the Deputy Prime Minister; then there was Mr. Dokmanovic, he was Minister of Agricultural; Bogdan Vorkapic as the Minister for Construction and Town Planning; Mr. Bogdan Vojnovic, who was the Minister of Finance; I think Mr. Bora Bogunovic was there as well as the Minister for Internal Affairs; I myself was present; and I think there were some other individuals, Assistant Ministers and Ministers as well. I'm afraid I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was Mr. Leskovac a member of the government? I realise he was not a Minister. Was he holding some other post for the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, in a way he was a member of the government because he was an Assistant Minister. As his Ministry, as I said earlier on, did not have a Deputy, then when Mr. Petrovic was absent, who was Minister for Information, Mr. Leskovac would perform his duties. And most frequently, Mr. Petrovic lived in Novi Sad. He was a fairly sick man, and so he was not present very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that Arkan was also present in this meeting. What was his role there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The role of Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan was fairly clear in a sense. Up to the beginning of the conflict in the area, his unit was first located in Tenia, and then after, some conflicts with some of our people from Tenia, they transferred to Erdut where he had ambitions of setting up a camp for the training -- a training camp for people who had to know about warfare and actually knew nothing about warfare. His relationship with Mr. Hadzic was a good one and very often he would give Mr. Hadzic -- he would supply security for Mr. Hadzic when he would travel through the region where the contact with enemy forces, hostile forces, was a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe in your statement to Mr. Waespi you also indicated that Major Sljivancanin joined the meeting at some point in time. What was the purpose for him coming to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin was not present at the meeting. If I remember correctly, I said on the occasion, and I'll repeat this, he turned up very briefly and left. But I met Mr. Sljivancanin twice in my life, but I saw him on television screens generally after the meeting. I think he just briefly entered and exited from the room. He did not discuss joining in our discussions, nor did he address us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated in the statement -- and I know the statement is in English. I'm not sure how well you can read English -- but on page 10 -- I'll read it out, and you can tell me if this is correct or incorrect. You said: "I think at that time Sljivancanin was present there too since he responded to my words saying that the army will take care of the prisoners of war exclusively."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: That was definitely stated by Mr. Vojnovic. If I said it as you have read it out, then I probably made a mistake. But Vojnovic spoke about that subject, and that I know full well to be a fact. Perhaps, in all this, I mixed up the statements made by Sljivancanin before or afterwards where he spoke about the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you say Major Sljivancanin was there briefly, are you indicating that he came into the meeting briefly but did not participate in discussions, or he was just outside at VELEPROMET?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I have the feeling that he did not come to the meeting at all, that he just came in to see who was there and went out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So this discussion in relation to prisoners of war took place with Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic exclusively?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I repeat, I think that his surname was Vojnovic, and if so, then that is the person in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you remember exactly what was discussed with him and who participated in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Not exactly, but basically, yes. As I said, Goran Hadzic took part in the discussion, Mladen Hadzic, Slavko Dokmanovic, myself. I think two or three other people took the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you can't recall exactly what was said?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Not exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were Territorial Defence commanders also present in this meeting on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I did not know all the Territorial Defence commanders, particularly the ones from Vukovar whom I met after Vukovar's liberation. It is possible that some of the commanders were there. There were several people in uniform whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you know Miroljub Vujovic or Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I met both of them after the operation to liberate Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As far as you can recall, neither one of them was present at this meeting on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I don't think they were there, no, not at the meeting. My acquaintance with them date to a later date, when they were cases brought to my court, before my court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And in the meantime, Mr. Vujovic was appointed to the executive council which governed the City of Vukovar, was he not?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I'm not sure that he was in the first team, but if he was, that would be no strange matter because he had exceptionally great authority in the area. We did not meddle in these matters too much, that is to say, who the people who had liberated Vukovar would send to the executive council. The only thing we wanted was that the President be Mr. Bibic of the executive council, who is a very calm elderly man whom we thought would have good organisational capabilities. He was a successful director, and we felt that a man of this kind would help us in achieving some good cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, after you came out of the meeting, you saw Mr. Dokmanovic again briefly outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I saw him for a brief moment outside. But it is possible that we passed each other. But that detail was such a minor detail that I don't think I can say when he left the courtyard, whether he stood in the courtyard, stood about for some time. I think that perhaps he did, but I can't quite remember where he was standing and when he left because all of us at one time left the courtyard, and, of course, all these people went through my line of vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So you are not aware of exactly when he left VELEPROMET or whom he left with?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I don't know who he left with. He might have left a little before me because the crowd started to thin at the time, and my driver took advantage of this occasion to introduce us into the column. And I think that his driver or anybody else driving did the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you did not see him again until you reached Orolik; correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And when you saw him, you said that Mr. Leskovac was with him. Was anybody else in his immediate company at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: There were several other individuals whom I was not acquainted with. I know Leskovac well, and so I saw him and took note of him immediately. Dokmanovic was in the forefront whereas Leskovac was a little behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see who Mr. Dokmanovic left Orolik with?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No. When this incident was over, and I hoped that I helped prevent it, we returned to the column, Dokmanovic was in front of us, and he left that place before us and turned towards Sid in the direction of Belgrade where we went too, but we didn't come across them anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you say he was in front of you, he was not immediately in front of you but, rather, he was far enough away that you weren't able to see what type of car he was in or who he was with or ...

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I couldn't say, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Susa. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I say something, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps just as a piece of information as to what we did during that period. I must say here before you today that the first case of trials for criminal cases was done in our court in Beli Manastir for war crimes where Boljevic was sentenced to a maximum sentence of 20 years' imprisonment, and I must also say that in the majority of cases we know exactly how people behaved on the terrain, and that my contact with the Croatian side was almost regular, and I am getting ready to go to Croatia next week to perform my duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I then ask you one question? These are cases brought before this court in Beli Manastir about crimes committed in the area of Vukovar in this particular period, '91, war crimes or ...

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The case that I mentioned was a war crime and it was committed in the Beli Manastir locality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: In the period between 1991 and '92, and the case was brought to trial in 1993 and '94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just based on this statement, I would just have a couple of follow-up questions, if I might?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined further by Mr. Williamson

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, this case that you are referring to, this was a man and his wife that lived in Beli Manastir; is that correct? And both of them were prosecuted in that case?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How many other prosecutions were brought, that you are aware of, against people for war crimes in the area?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that there were many cases of war crimes, but I must tell you that over 30 cases were tried for individual murders, and all these cases were conducted against Serbs for the crimes that they committed against Croats. But we had other cases as well, cases which we conducted against Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This case that you are referring to in Beli Manastir, what were the names of the accused in that matter?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I have to tell you that I did not follow all this in a direct manner because I never meddled with the affairs of the court, but the surname of the gentleman is Boljevic. I cannot remember his first name. Maybe I don't want to remember it. Anyhow, we have informed the international community in general, and Mr. Klein and his legal unit, we informed them about this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before I turn to Mr. Fila, I wonder whether the parties or the witness could provide the court with the judgements delivered in these particular cases, of course to the extent that they deal with war crimes. I think what the witness said is extremely interesting. I mean, if you may try to dig out all judgements and to provide a copy to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think it would be much easier for the Prosecution to get that, and I think that this man is still doing his time in Beli Manastir. He is still in prison. And my former chief of prison is still chief of prison there in Beli Manastir. And most of these people have remained and are still working for the judiciary in Croatia. It would be very easy for me to get that verdict, the judgement through Mr. Vasic or maybe through Judge Jelovac who was the President of the Trial Chamber, Presiding Judge. The Trial Chamber worked on this particular case. But this is a very known case, and I think that we informed there of all the -- all the important international entities, and I think that his sentence was confirmed by them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can say, if this is of some interest to the court, we can try to assist anyway we can, but the gentleman that he is talking about is not related in any way to any of the incidents which we have dealt with in this case, nor is he an individual whose name has come up at any point during our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. If you have the 20th of November in mind, no, he has nothing to do with it. No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any other investigations carried out for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Such as -- I don't want to state -- I don't know whether I am defending any of them.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who you are defending, but we conducted an investigation against a person by the name of Jurisic. There were several proceedings that were conducted, but not many of them reached the stage of, you know, war crimes trials. At that time, we were gathering facts that pointed to certain individual murders, and there were attempts to present these murders as some kind of revenge, as in attempts to gain some unlawful material again and things like that. This was very difficult for us to collect all the necessary facts and to prove the existence of a war crime, but we did complete all the work that was possible, and I can claim here on behalf of my colleagues as well that we worked professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me explain your status. You are now an attorney at law in Belgrade. Can you move freely in Croatia? Are there any proceedings that are being conducted against you in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Not that I know of. I went to Croatia several times and I still have very good contacts in Croatia and I am still on good terms with people there, and I go there without any fear and I will continue to do so in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, as a former Prosecutor and former Minister of Justice, of course you have special knowledge and you may be of great assistance to our court because I am sure that you have deep sensitivity to legal and institutional problems; so therefore, you can probably clarify some points. Let me ask you, first of all, about the relations between your government and the Republic of Serbia on one side and the central authorities in Belgrade between September '91 and January '92.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: I think that something has been misinterpreted. You spoke about Serbia, and the interpretation I got was the Republic of Serbia. Anyhow, I must tell you that my people found themselves in a very difficult position, and many people didn't know, didn't realise what was going on until a real tragedy befell them. At the beginning, it was the wish of the Republic of Croatia to create a sovereign and independent state and, on the other hand, there was the wish of Serbia to preserve Yugoslavia, and we were the ones who fared the worst in that kind of situation. We did not want to wage war together with the Republic of Croatia against our population, our people in Serbia. You can see that from a great number of people who had gone to Yugoslavia now want to go back to Croatia. This is not a time or place that I could enter into details which have nothing to do with my profession, but this was a great tragedy, and it is very difficult for people to live through such circumstances. These war crimes were committed by everyone. I do not wish to be more specific as to who these elements or people are. As for our relationship with the government in Belgrade, with the authorities in Belgrade, as long as we believed that Belgrade really wished to support us and that we had any realistic chances of remaining within Yugoslavia, although it was to be around Yugoslavia, our battle, our fight had some kind of meaning, and we wanted to prove our constitutional right that we had at that time within Yugoslavia. After Yugoslavia had established another state through the Zabljak constitution, everything became clear to us. I was aware of that even before. And people like myself experienced a lot of bad things. At that time we were not supposed to say publicly our opinion. I was not supposed to talk about things that were happening, and I couldn't permit myself such kind of behaviour. This situation is now perfectly clear. There are no longer Serbs in Croatia, and in Yugoslavia these people have not managed to find their place under the sun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Actually, let me explain why I asked you this question. In the minutes of the meeting of your government held on the 19th of November, it was stated at one point that one of the decisions was to set up a sort of meeting between the Republic of Serbia and the JNA, or to come to some sort of negotiations within the Republic of Serbia -- I'm saying Republic -- and the JNA. So I was interested in what sort of institutional relations your government had at that time with the Republic of Serbia, with the central authorities of the Republic of Serbia on the one side and with the authorities in Belgrade, of Yugoslavia. What sort of relations? Because, after all, you set up a government. You were a Minister of Justice in a government, and this government was an entity. I don't know whether it was an international entity, but it was an entity with Ministers, with a staff and so on, and functions, official functions. You were the Minister of Justice. So my query was about, as I say, the institutional relations between your government and two other governments, the government in Serbia and the government of the whole state, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1991 our ambition was, first and foremost, to have the competences of the federal authorities still present in the area where we lived. When we realised that this was not happening in a way that would provide us with some sort of protection, we did everything that's been discussed here for months; and in most aspects, it was the basic kind of self-protection. Later on, after we had established these bodies, when we were no longer within Yugoslavia, we wanted these bodies to be treated seriously and to be connected in an institutional manner, to have counterparts, to have discussions between governments, and this, unfortunately, never took place. I will mention my own example. The way I worked was, thanks to a number of people that I knew in the Ministry, and here I have the Ministry of Serbia in mind, who helped me with various kinds of material assistance and they would often invite me to their meetings where professional issues were discussed. But this was never brought to an official level of relations between two governments and two Ministries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, again I tried to rely on your legal background and experience. I wonder whether any objection was raised when you met in Vukovar on the 20th to the fact that the meeting was being presided over by somebody who was not part of your government, namely, a Colonel of the JNA, and I wonder whether you, as a Minister of Justice and as a lawyer, you felt that this was inappropriate for a meeting or an informal discussion of the government of this regional district of Slavonia and so on, to be presided over by a member of the JNA, of the army sent by Belgrade? Did anybody object to -- did you feel anything, that there was something inconsistent or odd in -- as I say, in a meeting not being presided over by the Prime Minister who, institutionally, should be the one who presides over a meeting of the whole government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Well, it was -- I was able to understand the fact that the conflict in Vukovar had just finished and the JNA had an active role in that conflict and it was still a war area, and I could understand that the army would play an important role. However, what I did not understand was the fact that we were discussing things with a man whom we had not known from before and who had a very low level within that structure, and my impression was that we were somehow being told about what our position was. I didn't want to attack this gentleman personally because I could tell that he was really embarrassed, and this I had in mind all the time. But in view of the situation in general, I think that Hadzic raised some kind of objection, and he said that he had a different idea of what that meeting should look like, and he said that he thought that we would be discussing some serious issues, and everything boiled down to the question of cleaning -- of the operations at the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You just said -- I am quoting your words: "I had the impression we were being told what our position was." May I infer from these words that you had the feeling that you were actually -- you, yourself, as the Minister of Justice, and the whole government, was under the control of military people, namely the JNA, and this was symbolically expressed by the fact that a Colonel of the JNA was presiding over the meeting, that in a way he was in charge of the meeting, he was controlling the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Even if we could agree that on that day everything remained within the realm of symbolism, I think that during those days it was perfectly clear and obvious, because on the roads that were controlled by the army, I had to have a written authorisation issued by military authorities for free movement. It is true that later on this was somehow simplified and I didn't have to have my pass every day. I could simply get an authorisation for movement for about five or six days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, was there any discussion in that meeting on the 20th of November about the plight of the civilians in the area of Vukovar, in Vukovar in particular, and with particular reference to all those civilians who had been detained by the army? Was there any discussion, what to do with those civilians, whether to take them away, whether to take them somewhere or to put them in camps? Was the issue discussed by the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: The issue was discussed, yes, but not by using the terms that you have just used. I don't know, and I didn't know at that time that civilians were being detained by the army. We were told that the army had under its control members of the Croatian National Guard, and that these people were supposed to be transported to Yugoslavia, which was okay, because we had no accommodation for these people. The only thing that was not right, and what we heard and which was confirmed later on, was that these people, without any proper criteria and prior determination as to their responsibility for crimes that were committed, whether they would be released and surrendered to the Croatian side. I'm sure that most of these people would fit that category, but it was also proved that in at least 10 cases there were war criminals within that group. As for the civilians, Dr. Mladen Hadzic, who is a very responsible doctor and a humanist, and I myself, we mentioned several times the need to evacuate women, children and elderly, so that the town would be liberated and so that we could start working on repairing the town itself. It was getting dark and I could not understand -- I could not accept the idea that people would spend the night in the open. It was already very cold, in spite of the fact that they had been -- the day had been quite sunny. Mr. Vojnovic kept convincing us that this was being taken care of and that this was the reason why buses were coming, and that people would be put in these buses and that they would be transported to one of the big sports halls which could accommodate a great number of people. Or that they would continue on their way to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, is there any particular legal or psychological reason why you as a former Prosecutor and Minister of Justice were wearing a military uniform? You said on the 20th you were wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was wearing a uniform. First of all, I was not able to wear anything better. My clothes had remained in Croatia and I did not want to wear clothes that are -- received from the Red Cross. Many of my friends and relatives were fighting and this was a sign of solidarity on my part, and in the area where I was, where I was staying, that uniform, believe me, is the most suitable type of clothing. Our life at that time seemed like a big adventure, and it was common for us to spend the night in the open at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. My final question, which is more general. It's about whether or not you felt during that meeting on the 20th of November, or afterwards that there was a sort of rift or dissension between extremists and moderates, whether somebody was putting pressures on one of the groups -- one of these two groups, whether extremists in particular were putting pressure on moderates to be tough because of public opinion, because of the shock, terrible shock, because you were all outraged by what you had seen in Vukovar, destruction, corpses lying everywhere, and of course this was terribly shocking to you. So I wonder whether, because of this shock, the extremists were putting some pressure on the moderates so as to prompt them to become tough and react in a different way to what had happened?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Whether people before that meeting, or after the meeting, discussed that amongst themselves, I cannot tell. I myself did not discuss with anyone the need of undertaking any radical measures to eliminating anyone. This was not discussed at the meeting. Nobody ever mentioned the way in which this whole thing would end and how the truth would be established as to what had happened during the past year. However, I myself was amongst those people who were in favour of establishing facts and finding out who committed crimes. And I did not make any distinction between Croats and Serbs at that time, nor am I making any distinction now. There were people on the Croat side who committed crimes against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You have not replied to my question. My question was whether or not you felt that there was some sort of pressure being put by the extremists on the moderates within the government, because I understand there were moderates, people who --

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA
utterances.text: Are you referring to the extremist within the government or extremists -- well, on that day during the meeting of the government, you couldn't find a single extremist who would go so far -- whether anyone at that time claimed that he was a Serb, and that this was very important for him at that time, yes I am one of them, but this is nothing to do with extremism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume there is no objection to the witness being released, Mr. Susa. Thank you so much for coming to give evidence here in court. You may now be released. We may adjourn now and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the expert opinion that I promised to you is now ready, and I hope that you have received it. You have? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You mean the expert assessment by Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I also have a statement for the witness who is scheduled for tomorrow. However, we don't have enough copies to give them -- to give it to you now. We'll have them tomorrow. The Prosecution has a copy of that statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you, who will come first tomorrow, the Colonel, Mr. Miodrag, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, Pavlovic followed by Mr. Dokmanovic, and I would kindly ask you -- for you to allow the presence of a psychiatrist during his testimony. And after that the psychiatrist will also testify. And this will conclude my case, as I promised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I had only a few minutes to quickly glance through the English text of the expert assessment by Dr. Petrovic, but I realise that there were quite a few pages about other witnesses. I assume Dr. Petrovic will only testify about the accused, not about the other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I have entrusted her with, she has responded to that. I don't know what you want to accept from her testimony and whatever we agree upon will be used during her testimony. In our system, when we request an expert assessment, I don't know how it works in your system, we have to provide her with a complete file, case file, so Dr. Petrovic has seen the indictment, everything that is not confidential, transcripts, videotapes of the interview with the accused, the detention unit, on the plane, statements of all witnesses who have been heard so far, and who are not under any protection order. And on the basis of that she provides her opinion about the accused, about nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course we are not going to apply other Italian or British or some other law. We are applying International law, International criminal law. We discussed -- had a very brief discussion before entering the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but there was no other way for me to request for this expert analysis. That's what I am trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We want you to confirm -- to make it clear to Dr. Petrovic that of course her expert assessment must be confined to a psychological or psychiatric evaluation of Mr. Dokmanovic. That's all. Nothing to do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's fine with us, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Because she cannot -- she is not authorised to say anything about witnesses who have been heard by the court. So only, therefore -- and probably we will accept only the statement to the extent that it deals with Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the reason why I have provided you with this beforehand, because you are creating a new system here and if I were to give this to you a minute before the hearing, we wouldn't accomplish anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. Any comments? All right. So we will now adjourn and we'll start again tomorrow at 9.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All rise.
